## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools … [truncated]

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`; the `alexandria` and `requestId` parameters describe batching, retries, errors and provider terms. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Identifies one logical Alexandria execution; generated when omitted and returned with the result. Repeated attempts of the identical payload require the same ID. A new ID cannot reconcile a pending or uncertain execution. A caller-supplied ID supports recovery if no response is received. Errors relay a code and may include chargeId. request_in_flight (409) means the execution is pending; request_unresolved (503) requires reconciliation under the same ID; duplicate_request (409) means the ID belongs to a different payload; unknown_provider (404), insufficient_credits (402) and billing_unavailable (503) mean nothing executed.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. nextTool identifies access to retained results without repeating a successful provider call. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. THIRD_PARTY_DATA_TERMS_REQUIRED (403) means execution is blocked by provider terms, with requiresAction.url for review by an organization admin. Through this tool, terms/show displays the agreement and terms/accept records acceptance; acceptance requires explicit user authorization for the reviewed version and digest and confirmed:true. A data request does not authorize acceptance. Provider execution remains blocked until acceptance is confirmed.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

# Knowledge-Behaviour Self-Audit

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Started 2026-09-25. Professional development folder item, due 2026-09-30.

Source: Old Bull Performance, *Running The Room*, Module 1, Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook (sections B1 to B3 and D1). Private. Section C (rating other people) is deliberately not done.

## The two axes

- **Knowledge:** Handbrake, Pawn, Practitioner, Operator. An Operator can design, integrate and troubleshoot complex systems and sees how technology, training and operations connect.
- **Behaviour:** Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst. A Catalyst creates movement, influences others, and finds the path forward.

## B1. Where I sit now

**Knowledge: Practitioner.**
I understand our tools, our context and our environment. I can help solve problems, build frameworks, and have useful conversations about them. Where I stall is the last step of execution. I have many ideas and many ways to integrate things at a conceptual and theoretical level, but getting them over the final hump into something that bears fruit is where I fall short. By the course's own test, I am not yet an Operator: the systems I build would not keep running without me.

**Behaviour: Catalyst in effort, not yet in outcome.**
I work to create movement and influence others: I mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas to leadership, put together solution proposals, learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of that back here, and bring new ideas and organisational structures into the conversation. But when I ask whether the change sticks, the honest answer is often no. The workbook offers only three levels and I am clearly not a Coaster, so Catalyst is the placement, with the caveat that my evidence is mostly inputs (proposals, presentations, conversations) rather than changes that lasted.

**The common thread.** Both axes point at the same gap: turning ideas into things that run and last without me. That gap separates Practitioner from Operator, and it is also what separates pushing for change from change that sticks.

## B2. Evidence

**Knowledge (what I actually do):**
- Built the football GPS and force-plate data pipelines myself.
- Built the PFF database and the EPA matchup profiles used in weekly game preparation.
- Designed the volleyball monitoring framework with Coach Mike Wenger so that he runs it end to end: he collects, cleans, exports and imports the data. My part is routine maintenance and one spreadsheet button he could press himself. This is the one system I have built that would keep running without me, which is the Operator test.

**Behaviour (how I show up):**
- Mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas and solution proposals to leadership.
- Learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of it back here.
- **What stuck:** the volleyball framework. It was built with its daily user, and he owns it.
- **What faded:** the technology framework and much of the reporting we discussed; the DEXA project on using body composition to profile athlete potential; a website; a newsletter; an auditing framework for departmental objectives. Each was pushed early and went nowhere.

**Why the difference.** The one that stuck had a co-owner from the start who used it every day and needed it. The ones that faded were mine alone: no one else to support them, carry them or ask for them. I have been trying to get things off the ground by myself, without much success. I need a co-pilot, a co-champion attached to each project who has real weight behind it.

## B3. Where I want to be in 3 to 5 years

**Knowledge: Operator. Behaviour: Catalyst, in outcome and not only in effort.**

**What would need to change:** I need to start shipping. I have a whiteboard full of ideas, projects and tasks. I need to see them through to completion in an ordered way, push them out, and expose people to them, instead of keeping a half-finished list that nobody else knows about, which is where I am now. The principle is "Always Be Shipping," from Seth Godin's idea of shipping: finish the idea, put it in front of people, move on to the next one. Some of what I ship will stick, or grow from other people's input, and turn from a one-off project into something sustainable. At the least it creates value, and the visible sense of value, so that others here and at other institutions pick up on it and I can help where I am needed.

**The check from B2:** shipping alone to no one is how the five faded projects died. So each thing I ship goes to a named person who will use it, the way the volleyball framework went to Coach Wenger. Ship to someone, not into the air.

## D1. Three actions in the next 30 to 90 days

Goal: move one step on each axis, from shipping ideas to shipping things that other people use and keep using.

1. **Ship one piece every two weeks, to a named person.** Before I start anything, I write down who will use it. If no one would, it doesn't get picked. Each item ships as a small first piece, not the whole project.
2. **Record every ship in the "Shipped" section of the biweekly status report:** what it was, who got it, the date. This makes the work visible to Chris and Kenny without extra effort.
3. **Check whether it stuck, 30 days after each ship.** One question to the person who got it: "Are you still using it?" That measures the outcome, not the effort.

**Ship queue (first three):**

| # | Project | Who uses it | First piece to ship | Target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Education initiative: weekly research report and slide deck in MS Teams | Staff and student-athletes | Research in 5 #002 (v2 already built), then weekly | Week of Sept 28 |
| 2 | Internship curriculum | Interns and the intern supervisor | Module 1, handed to the supervisor to run | Oct 9 |
| 3 | Applied Performance Digest: department handbook and operations manual, including items that meet the NCAA technology recommendations | Applied Performance staff | One chapter: one device procedure (ForceDecks CMJ), in the handbook format | Oct 23 |

30-day stick checks fall about Oct 28, Nov 8 and Nov 22.

## Status

Complete 2026-09-25. Private: not shared, not in any repo.

# RTP_Constraints_Course

A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).

**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
phase of return to performance in American football.

## How to work here

Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.

Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |
| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |
| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. 0001 written 2026-09-03 (opposed vs unopposed). |
| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. |
| `reference/gray-infographics/` | Local copies of Rob Gray's free infographics, saved 2026-09-03 because the site is one person's. Includes the 21-study comparative table, extracted and searchable. **Do not republish, do not commit.** See its `README.md`. |
| `sources/` | Full-text books and long PDFs obtained legitimately. Author-supplied — **never redistribute, never commit.** Holds the Myszka book (240 pages, printed 14–253), its OCR text sidecar, the reversible scan manifest, and the extracted bibliography. |
| `scripts/` | The book-scan pipeline. `scan_pipeline.py` turns phone photos into a page-ordered OCR'd PDF and **refuses to rename unless the arithmetic gate passes**; `verify_pdf.py` proves page order afterwards by an independent route. Read `scan_pipeline.py`'s docstring before the next scanning job — it carries every trap found so far. |
| `docs/handoffs/` | Durable cross-session handoffs. Newest first. |
| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. 0001 records the lesson-0001 hook decision and Joe's starting floor. |

## Rules specific to this workspace

- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.
- **Every lesson ends in something Joe could do at practice tomorrow.**
- `GLOSSARY.md` does not exist yet by design — see `NOTES.md`.
- **Phase 2 is a drill-design tool.** Do not start it until the lessons have specified it.
  Route: `/grill-with-docs` → `/prototype` → `/implement`. Local-only per Baylor IT.

## Source library

Papers referenced as `LIB/…` live in `~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/research-papers/`.
Search with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`. Zotero MCP was down on 2026-09-01.
# STATUS

## Current state
- The Myszka book has printed pages 1–253 in one verified PDF.
- PDF page numbers match printed page numbers.
- All 10 chapters already have 84 library entries.

## Next
- Import `sources/myszka-references-new.ris` into Zotero.
- Write lesson 0002.

## Open questions
- None.

## Gotchas
- Keep the book PDF and OCR text local and ignored by Git.
- Do not scan pages 254 onward. They add no course material.
- Do not run a second book ingest.
# Mission: Constraints-Led Return to Performance (American Football)

> **Confirmed with Joe on 2026-09-03**, in a 47.8-minute mission interview run from
> `INTERVIEW.md`. Every claim below traces to something Joe said. Source and timestamps:
> `interviews/2026-09-03-joe-smith-mission-interview.md`.
> Quoted lines are Joe's own words.

## Why

Joe Smith (assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics) wants to own return to
performance at Baylor football. In his words: *"I want to be known as the guy in this
room that does return to performance… and that I make our football team better by the
return to performance that the guys complete."*

He draws a hard line between **return to play** and **return to performance**. Return to
play is when drills begin to look and feel like football. Return to performance is when
you are chasing back the level the player actually held before. His test for it: *"I
could go out there and play football. I would not be expected to perform at the same
level that our guys are."* He wants that distinction written into the Baylor framework,
and says the sheet already in use has room for it.

What he is not asking for is a way to fill the post-clearance gap. **He explicitly
rejected that boundary.** The work starts at the back end of rehab, before clearance, and
it also covers acute cases — players who are never held out at all, which is most of what
he does day to day.

The method he already runs is a needs assessment, then a **reverse calendar** worked
backwards from the target event, then density and intensity set per day. That method is
sound and stays. What it lacks is a defensible account of *why* a given exposure is the
right one — and that is the gap this course fills.

The sharpest thing Joe said about his own weakness: *"I'm least confident in the ability
to rationalize a very subjective process to objectively oriented people."*

**That sentence is the mission.** Joe does not need convincing that this work matters. He
needs language, structure and evidence that survive a hostile question from someone who
was not there.

## Success looks like

- Joe can explain to a skeptical position coach why a pre-planned cone drill is not evidence of readiness.
- **Joe can defend a subjective judgement to an objective audience** — naming the information the athlete had to use, the problem the exposure posed, and why the result counts as evidence. This is the one that matters most to him.
- Joe can name the three constraint classes — performer, task, environment — and deliberately manipulate each to raise or lower a drill's demand.
- **Joe can say why his non-reactive drills flatter an athlete**, and design the reactive exposure that finds what they hide. He has already seen this happen with a returning offensive lineman; he does not yet have the vocabulary for it.
- Joe can state, for a given position and injury, what perceptual information that job actually requires, and judge whether a drill samples it (representative design).
- Joe can build a progression from controlled to chaotic and say out loud where a given athlete sits on it, and why.
- **Joe can name when he is not the right constraint.** He cannot load a lineman at his own size, and had to bring in a position coach and real bodies to finish that case. He should be able to say when a person, not a drill, is the missing piece.
- Joe can apply all of the above in the **acute** case, not only after a long rehab.
- Joe can spec a session in under 10 minutes using the drill-design tool built at the end of this course.

## Constraints

- **Joe is a clinician, not a researcher.** Lessons must be short, practical, and free of statistics-heavy reading.
- **Time: about 4 hours a week in season, spread across 7 days; 3–4 hours across 5 days off season.** Confirmed by Joe.
- **He learns badly in fragments.** *"I want to take notes, I want to like reread… really think about something to truly understand it."* A lesson billed at 20 minutes will cost him 30–35. **Size lessons for the way he actually works, not for the clock.**
- **Feedback must coach, not just correct.** *"I love to know when I'm wrong, and I'd love to be coached… if you're gonna tell me I'm wrong, I want to know how to fix it."* Never flag an error without a route out of it.
- **Starting knowledge is zero.** Ecological dynamics: he has heard the term only from Eric. CLA: heard of it, never implemented it, holds no opinion. Assume nothing.
- **Joe does not own medical clearance.** The method has to slot into the existing physician/ATC chain, not replace it. Jacob (director of rehab) and Tim (head athletic trainer) are the gatekeepers.
- **It must survive people who were not in the room.** Expect two objections: that a dedicated person is a poor use of resources because every athletic trainer should run return-to-play progressions, and that this should be a weight-room collaboration instead. Joe needs an answer to both.
- **American football only.** Position-specific, contact sport, high chaos. Every position, quarterback to kicker.
- **Delivery:** at his laptop, in the office. All standard equipment available. GPS, force plates and force frame are available and are not a limiter. He is willing to film sessions.
- **Tool must run locally** — no cloud services or servers without Baylor IT approval.
- Eric Rash commissions and steers this; Joe is the learner. **Confirmed 2026-09-03** — Joe asked whether Eric intends to do this for other young professionals, and is treating it as a career move rather than a favour.

## Out of scope

- Early-stage rehabilitation, tissue healing timelines, and the criteria for medical clearance itself. **The course does cover the back end of rehab before clearance — it just does not decide clearance.**
- Motor-learning theory disputes (schema theory vs. ecological) beyond the minimum needed to defend a drill.
- Sports other than American football.
- Building a full athlete-management system. The deliverable is one focused drill-design tool.
- Cases with no performance level to rebuild. Joe's own example is rhabdomyolysis: an evaluation question, not a return-to-performance one.

## The drill-design tool — Joe's specification

Recorded from the interview so it is not lost. **Do not build it yet; the lessons specify
it.** Full detail with timestamps in the interview digest.

**Inputs:** injury type, split structural/mechanical (watch shifting, popping, clicking)
versus muscle belly (watch pain, tension, tightness) · previous exposure and the response
to it, his read and the athlete's · the needs assessment · the target event, including
sub-events on a long rehab.

**Outputs:** a reverse calendar of the progression — **explicitly not "gradual"**, because
Joe wants spikes, hills and valleys and treats the response to a spike as information ·
research-backed numbers where they exist, particularly return-to-run and high-speed
running for hamstrings · density and intensity blocks that undulate with the team week
(Tue/Wed high, Thu low, Fri/Sat up), which he admits he currently does sporadically · a
checklist of qualities covered — reactive and non-reactive, explosive and non-explosive,
joint angles, plus an aerobic/anaerobic layer · if-yes/if-no branches, so there is a plan
B when the athlete presents differently than expected.

**It does not go in the EMR.** It is an aid; Joe writes his note afterwards anyway.

## What would make Joe walk

Not the learning — he said nothing would take him away from the work itself. What would
take him away from doing it **here** is the value being recognised by the people close to
it in football, and not matched by support from outside that circle.

**Implication for this course:** the artefacts have to travel. Something Joe can hand to
someone who was never at the practice is not a nice-to-have.

# Mission: Constraints-Led Return to Performance (American Football)

> **Confirmed with Joe on 2026-09-03**, in a 47.8-minute mission interview run from
> `INTERVIEW.md`. Every claim below traces to something Joe said. Source and timestamps:
> `interviews/2026-09-03-joe-smith-mission-interview.md`.
> Quoted lines are Joe's own words.

## Why

Joe Smith (assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics) wants to own return to
performance at Baylor football. In his words: *"I want to be known as the guy in this
room that does return to performance… and that I make our football team better by the
return to performance that the guys complete."*

He draws a hard line between **return to play** and **return to performance**. Return to
play is when drills begin to look and feel like football. Return to performance is when
you are chasing back the level the player actually held before. His test for it: *"I
could go out there and play football. I would not be expected to perform at the same
level that our guys are."* He wants that distinction written into the Baylor framework,
and says the sheet already in use has room for it.

What he is not asking for is a way to fill the post-clearance gap. **He explicitly
rejected that boundary.** The work starts at the back end of rehab, before clearance, and
it also covers acute cases — players who are never held out at all, which is most of what
he does day to day.

The method he already runs is a needs assessment, then a **reverse calendar** worked
backwards from the target event, then density and intensity set per day. That method is
sound and stays. What it lacks is a defensible account of *why* a given exposure is the
right one — and that is the gap this course fills.

The sharpest thing Joe said about his own weakness: *"I'm least confident in the ability
to rationalize a very subjective process to objectively oriented people."*

**That sentence is the mission.** Joe does not need convincing that this work matters. He
needs language, structure and evidence that survive a hostile question from someone who
was not there.

## Success looks like

- Joe can explain to a skeptical position coach why a pre-planned cone drill is not evidence of readiness.
- **Joe can defend a subjective judgement to an objective audience** — naming the information the athlete had to use, the problem the exposure posed, and why the result counts as evidence. This is the one that matters most to him.
- Joe can name the three constraint classes — performer, task, environment — and deliberately manipulate each to raise or lower a drill's demand.
- **Joe can say why his non-reactive drills flatter an athlete**, and design the reactive exposure that finds what they hide. He has already seen this happen with a returning offensive lineman; he does not yet have the vocabulary for it.
- Joe can state, for a given position and injury, what perceptual information that job actually requires, and judge whether a drill samples it (representative design).
- Joe can build a progression from controlled to chaotic and say out loud where a given athlete sits on it, and why.
- **Joe can name when he is not the right constraint.** He cannot load a lineman at his own size, and had to bring in a position coach and real bodies to finish that case. He should be able to say when a person, not a drill, is the missing piece.
- Joe can apply all of the above in the **acute** case, not only after a long rehab.
- Joe can spec a session in under 10 minutes using the drill-design tool built at the end of this course.

## Constraints

- **Joe is a clinician, not a researcher.** Lessons must be short, practical, and free of statistics-heavy reading.
- **Time: about 4 hours a week in season, spread across 7 days; 3–4 hours across 5 days off season.** Confirmed by Joe.
- **He learns badly in fragments.** *"I want to take notes, I want to like reread… really think about something to truly understand it."* A lesson billed at 20 minutes will cost him 30–35. **Size lessons for the way he actually works, not for the clock.**
- **Feedback must coach, not just correct.** *"I love to know when I'm wrong, and I'd love to be coached… if you're gonna tell me I'm wrong, I want to know how to fix it."* Never flag an error without a route out of it.
- **Starting knowledge is zero.** Ecological dynamics: he has heard the term only from Eric. CLA: heard of it, never implemented it, holds no opinion. Assume nothing.
- **Joe does not own medical clearance.** The method has to slot into the existing physician/ATC chain, not replace it. Jacob (director of rehab) and Tim (head athletic trainer) are the gatekeepers.
- **It must survive people who were not in the room.** Expect two objections: that a dedicated person is a poor use of resources because every athletic trainer should run return-to-play progressions, and that this should be a weight-room collaboration instead. Joe needs an answer to both.
- **American football only.** Position-specific, contact sport, high chaos. Every position, quarterback to kicker.
- **Delivery:** at his laptop, in the office. All standard equipment available. GPS, force plates and force frame are available and are not a limiter. He is willing to film sessions.
- **Tool must run locally** — no cloud services or servers without Baylor IT approval.
- Eric Rash commissions and steers this; Joe is the learner. **Confirmed 2026-09-03** — Joe asked whether Eric intends to do this for other young professionals, and is treating it as a career move rather than a favour.

## Out of scope

- Early-stage rehabilitation, tissue healing timelines, and the criteria for medical clearance itself. **The course does cover the back end of rehab before clearance — it just does not decide clearance.**
- Motor-learning theory disputes (schema theory vs. ecological) beyond the minimum needed to defend a drill.
- Sports other than American football.
- Building a full athlete-management system. The deliverable is one focused drill-design tool.
- Cases with no performance level to rebuild. Joe's own example is rhabdomyolysis: an evaluation question, not a return-to-performance one.

## The drill-design tool — Joe's specification

Recorded from the interview so it is not lost. **Do not build it yet; the lessons specify
it.** Full detail with timestamps in the interview digest.

**Inputs:** injury type, split structural/mechanical (watch shifting, popping, clicking)
versus muscle belly (watch pain, tension, tightness) · previous exposure and the response
to it, his read and the athlete's · the needs assessment · the target event, including
sub-events on a long rehab.

**Outputs:** a reverse calendar of the progression — **explicitly not "gradual"**, because
Joe wants spikes, hills and valleys and treats the response to a spike as information ·
research-backed numbers where they exist, particularly return-to-run and high-speed
running for hamstrings · density and intensity blocks that undulate with the team week
(Tue/Wed high, Thu low, Fri/Sat up), which he admits he currently does sporadically · a
checklist of qualities covered — reactive and non-reactive, explosive and non-explosive,
joint angles, plus an aerobic/anaerobic layer · if-yes/if-no branches, so there is a plan
B when the athlete presents differently than expected.

**It does not go in the EMR.** It is an aid; Joe writes his note afterwards anyway.

## What would make Joe walk

Not the learning — he said nothing would take him away from the work itself. What would
take him away from doing it **here** is the value being recognised by the people close to
it in football, and not matched by support from outside that circle.

**Implication for this course:** the artefacts have to travel. Something Joe can hand to
someone who was never at the practice is not a nice-to-have.

 frameworks
 A framework is the backbone of
 on-field rehab. It provides structure,
 consistency, and efficiency, but it is not a rigid protocol. Instead, it acts as a guide that
 balances evidence with practitioner experience, allowing you to adapt to the needs of
 the individual athlete and the context of their injury. A good framework helps you
 manage risk, align rehab with the actual demands of sport, and make decisions quickly
 and confidently.
Sportsmith
  Why frameworks matter
 There are four key benefits to using a framework in on-field rehab. First, it allows
 you to take calculated risks. Rehab is never risk-free, but a framework acts like
 guardrails, ensuring you avoid progressing too quickly and causing a recurrence.
 Second, when a framework mirrors the performance requirements of sport, it
 enhances preparedness for return to play. Third, frameworks build in flexibility.
 They are not step-by-step manuals but adaptable guides that can be individualized
 for each athlete. And finally, they promote efficiency and consistency. With a
 structured approach, you can build programs faster, prescribe exercises with
 confidence, and make better decisions on the fly, all of which increase athlete trust
 in the process.
 Levels of on-field rehab
 On-field rehab can be split into levels that move progressively from controlled,
 low-intensity work to chaotic, high-intensity, game-like situations. These levels
 typically sit within the mid-to-late stages of rehab:
 Early stage: Gym-based work before progressing to the field.
 Mid-stage: Often broken into on-field rehab levels 1, 2, and 3.
 Late stage: Levels 4 and 5, leading into team training and return to play.
 For example, in the hamstring case study, the athlete completed one session at
 each level because of the injury's mild nature. With more severe injuries, multiple
 sessions at each level may be required. The athlete then transitioned into team
 training sessions before being cleared for competition.
 This level-based structure scaffolds the athlete's gradual exposure to the
 locomotive actions of their sport, ensuring intensity and complexity build
 systematically.
 Progressing intensity and complexity
 Two objectives drive the progression process: intensity and complexity.
 Intensity begins with competency. Athletes are reintroduced to locomotive
 actions, sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, changing direction, and
 submaximal running, at low to moderate speeds. Over time, the focus shifts to
 capacity, where the athlete must tolerate higher intensities and volumes until
 they can handle maximum velocity and repeated exposures.
 Complexity is best understood through the control-to-chaos continuum
 popularized by Matt Tabiner. Early sessions are highly controlled and low-risk.
 As athletes progress, the environment becomes less predictable, moving toward
 "chaos", highly reactive, game-like situations. Complexity is increased by
 manipulating variables such as space, opposition, and task constraints, creating

1	=========== PART 1 PDF
2	 COURSES
3	the
4	fundamentals
5	of on-field
6	rehabilitation
7	 Sportsmith
8	  Hi everybody,
9	 my name is Simon Harries.
10	 Thanks for joining us and I'm delighted to
11	 partner with Sportsmith to bring you this
12	 course where we are going to get into how I
13	 approach on-field rehab.
14	 The aim of this course is to give you the
15	 frameworks and tools to improve your on-
16	 field rehabilitation practices. To bring to life
17	 I will be presenting 3 in-depth case studies
18	 and allow you to see the commonalities
19	 across injuries
20	 Let's get going!
21	 Course introduction
22	 Rehab running, or on-field rehabilitation, is the crucial bridge between gym-based
23	 rehab and a full return to sport. Its purpose goes beyond healing the injured
24	 structure. It prepares the athlete to meet the technical, tactical, and physical
25	 demands of competition. This stage typically begins with the athlete's first steps
26	 back into running and progresses through increasingly complex and demanding
27	 scenarios. A structured framework ensures that the athlete regains locomotive and
28	 physical qualities while minimizing the risk of flare-ups or re-injury.
29	 On-field rehab has two primary objectives:
30	 Fully rehabilitating the injured area
31	 Preparing the athlete to handle the realities of their sport
32	 It is not enough to restore function in isolation. The athlete must also be
33	 conditioned to execute technical and tactical tasks under game-like intensity.
34	Sportsmith
35	  Managing risk is central to this process. Training loads must be progressed
36	 carefully to avoid negative responses such as soreness, tightness, or recurrence of
37	 the original injury. Success depends on clarity. You must know what physical and
38	 locomotive activities the athlete's sport demands and how to progress their ability
39	 to perform them safely and specifically.
40	 Finding common ground across team sports
41	 One of the biggest challenges in designing an on-field rehab framework is the sheer
42	 variety of actions performed in sport. Footballers dribble and press, rugby players
43	 tackle and pass, and basketball players cut and pivot. Yet, despite these surface
44	 differences, invasion-based sports all share the same tactical patterns: teams attack
45	 by creating and invading space, and they defend by protecting or closing space.
46	 Technical actions also overlap, such as carrying or passing a ball, pressing an
47	 opponent, or recovering into position.
48	 At the foundation of these tactical and technical actions lie a handful of locomotive
49	 tasks that never change. Sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, and changing
50	 direction are the common denominators of performance across team sports. These
51	 four actions form the locomotive pillars of on-field rehab. Regardless of the sport,
52	 you can build progression frameworks around these pillars and then layer technical
53	 or tactical context on top. For example, an acceleration drill may be progressed into
54	 a pressing scenario, while deceleration can be integrated into a defensive recovery
55	 pattern.
56	 Three pillars of on-field rehab
57	 All sound on-field rehab frameworks can be built around these three major themes:
58	 Submaximal and maximal velocity running
59	 Athletes must be gradually exposed to increasing speeds, culminating in repeated
60	 exposures at sprint velocity before they are ready to compete
61	 Multi-directional speed and agility
62	 Here, the athlete rehearses accelerations, decelerations, and changes of direction
63	 under increasing load, eventually re-creating the movement patterns required in
64	 offensive and defensive scenarios
65	 Sport-specific skills
66	 Technical and tactical tasks, passing, pressing, contesting, carrying must be layered
67	 onto locomotive drills so the athlete can demonstrate physical and skill execution
68	 together in realistic game contexts.
69	Sportsmith
70	  Putting the framework into practice
71	 The first step in applying these principles is to audit the sport in question. Break it
72	 down into technical, tactical, and physical domains, then identify the overlaps and
73	 commonalities. From there, anchor your framework on the four locomotive pillars;
74	 sprinting, acceleration, deceleration, and change of direction. Progression is about
75	 gradually increasing both the intensity and the complexity of tasks. Start with
76	 submaximal efforts and controlled environments, then move toward maximal
77	 outputs in chaotic, game-like contexts. Incorporate offensive and defensive
78	 scenarios so that physical tasks are performed for tactical purposes, such as creating
79	 space in attack or closing space in defense. Throughout the process, closely
80	 monitor the athlete's response. Signs of overload which are tightness, fatigue, or
81	 symptom recurrence should trigger an adjustment to the plan. Finally, use the
82	 athlete's competitive benchmarks as your guide. Re-exposure to sprint distance,
83	 high-speed running volumes, and repeated accelerations should all be achieved
84	 before the athlete is cleared for full return.
85	 Rehab running is far more than simply getting an athlete back to jogging. It is a
86	 structured, progressive, and context-driven process that reconnects the athlete with
87	 the locomotive, technical, and tactical demands of their sport. By grounding your
88	 framework in universal pillars, progressing tasks from simple to complex, and
89	 ensuring benchmarks are met, you can safely and effectively guide athletes from the
90	 gym back onto the field with confidence.
91	 Let's move onto part 2.
92	Sportsmith
93	=========== PART 2 PDF
94	 COURSES
95	 the
96	 fundamentals
97	 of on-field
98	 rehabilitation
99	 Part 2
100	 On-field rehab
101	 frameworks
102	 A framework is the backbone of
103	 on-field rehab. It provides structure,
104	 consistency, and efficiency, but it is not a rigid protocol. Instead, it acts as a guide that
105	 balances evidence with practitioner experience, allowing you to adapt to the needs of
106	 the individual athlete and the context of their injury. A good framework helps you
107	 manage risk, align rehab with the actual demands of sport, and make decisions quickly
108	 and confidently.
109	Sportsmith
110	  Why frameworks matter
111	 There are four key benefits to using a framework in on-field rehab. First, it allows
112	 you to take calculated risks. Rehab is never risk-free, but a framework acts like
113	 guardrails, ensuring you avoid progressing too quickly and causing a recurrence.
114	 Second, when a framework mirrors the performance requirements of sport, it
115	 enhances preparedness for return to play. Third, frameworks build in flexibility.
116	 They are not step-by-step manuals but adaptable guides that can be individualized
117	 for each athlete. And finally, they promote efficiency and consistency. With a
118	 structured approach, you can build programs faster, prescribe exercises with
119	 confidence, and make better decisions on the fly, all of which increase athlete trust
120	 in the process.
121	 Levels of on-field rehab
122	 On-field rehab can be split into levels that move progressively from controlled,
123	 low-intensity work to chaotic, high-intensity, game-like situations. These levels
124	 typically sit within the mid-to-late stages of rehab:
125	 Early stage: Gym-based work before progressing to the field.
126	 Mid-stage: Often broken into on-field rehab levels 1, 2, and 3.
127	 Late stage: Levels 4 and 5, leading into team training and return to play.
128	 For example, in the hamstring case study, the athlete completed one session at
129	 each level because of the injury's mild nature. With more severe injuries, multiple
130	 sessions at each level may be required. The athlete then transitioned into team
131	 training sessions before being cleared for competition.
132	 This level-based structure scaffolds the athlete's gradual exposure to the
133	 locomotive actions of their sport, ensuring intensity and complexity build
134	 systematically.
135	 Progressing intensity and complexity
136	 Two objectives drive the progression process: intensity and complexity.
137	 Intensity begins with competency. Athletes are reintroduced to locomotive
138	 actions, sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, changing direction, and
139	 submaximal running, at low to moderate speeds. Over time, the focus shifts to
140	 capacity, where the athlete must tolerate higher intensities and volumes until
141	 they can handle maximum velocity and repeated exposures.
142	 Complexity is best understood through the control-to-chaos continuum
143	 popularized by Matt Tabiner. Early sessions are highly controlled and low-risk.
144	 As athletes progress, the environment becomes less predictable, moving toward
145	 "chaos", highly reactive, game-like situations. Complexity is increased by
146	 manipulating variables such as space, opposition, and task constraints, creating
147	 more realistic environments for decision-making and movement execution.
148	Sportsmith
149	  A common misconception is that each new level automatically means more chaos
150	 across all drills. In reality, progression is gradual. Some actions may still require
151	 controlled environments at higher intensities, while others are ready to be tested
152	 under chaotic, game-like conditions. Intensity and complexity must be treated as
153	 separate but equally important goals.
154	 Control to chaos in practice
155	 The continuum is not simply about intensity or randomness, it is about preparing
156	 athletes to act effectively under the same uncertainty they will face in competition.
157	 At the controlled end, you structure the environment tightly, focusing on safe
158	 reintroduction of movement. At the chaotic end, drills replicate unpredictable
159	 scenarios where athletes must choose and execute the right action under pressure.
160	 This progression demands careful design. Using constraint-based learning
161	 principles, you can manipulate the task, the environment, or the individual's role to
162	 adjust the level of complexity. Over time, the ratio shifts: more work is performed
163	 in chaotic settings while less remains in tightly controlled conditions.
164	 End-stage rehab: competitive demands
165	 At the end of the process, athletes must be able to combine high intensity with high
166	 complexity. This is not just about physical readiness but also about confidence and
167	 decision-making. An athlete should be willing to sprint into space, accelerate to
168	 chase down an opponent, or react decisively in a chaotic small-sided game. If they
169	 hesitate in these competitive situations, they are not ready to return.
170	 In other words, the final stage of rehab is not optional chaos, it is essential.
171	 Exposing athletes to competitive, high-risk, and high-intensity scenarios is the only
172	 way to ensure they are prepared for the realities of their sport.
173	 Conclusion
174	 Frameworks bring order to the messy reality of on-field rehab. By breaking the
175	 process into progressive levels and systematically increasing both intensity and
176	 complexity, you create a safe and effective pathway back to competition. The
177	 ultimate goal is simple: an athlete who is physically prepared, mentally confident,
178	 and capable of executing high-intensity actions in chaotic, competitive
179	 environments. Anything less leaves them underprepared for the demands of sport.
180	Sportsmith
181	=========== PART 3 PDF
182	 COURSES
183	 the
184	 fundamentals
185	 of on-field
186	 rehabilitation
187	 Part 3
188	 Linear submaximal &
189	 maximal running
190	 progressions
191	 The first major pillar of on-field rehab
192	 is the progression from submaximal to
193	 maximal running velocity. This pillar begins with preparing the athlete to return to
194	 running and continues through jogging, running, striding, and ultimately sprinting.
195	 Each step involves increasing intensity and mechanical demand, so a structured and
196	 careful progression is essential.
197	Sportsmith
198	  Understanding running velocities
199	 Running speed categories can be broken down into clear ranges:
200	 Walking: <6 km/h, less than 25% of max velocity.
201	 Sprinting: >27 km/h, above 85% of max velocity.
202	 As speed increases, vertical ground reaction forces grow larger, contact times get
203	 shorter, and muscular power demands rise--especially at the hip, knee, and ankle.
204	 This has implications for injury-specific rehab: ankle-dominant strategies are more
205	 relevant at lower speeds, while hip-dominant mechanics dominate as athletes
206	 approach striding and sprinting.
207	 Preparation for running
208	 Before progressing into steady-state running, athletes should demonstrate
209	 competence in drills that reintroduce upright running mechanics and repetitive
210	 impact cycles. These include:
211	 Dribble walks and runs (over ankle, shin, and knee height) to reinforce front-
212	 side mechanics.
213	 Skipping drills (e.g., A-skips) to add stiffness and reactivity.
214	 Low-intensity jumping such as pogos and unilateral hops for repetitive loading.
215	 Scissor shuffles and bounds to target aggressive hip flexion and extension.
216	 These preparatory drills serve both as warm-ups and readiness assessments,
217	 ensuring athletes can tolerate dynamic impact and postural demands before
218	 progressing.
219	 Progressing running speed
220	 The transition from jogging to sprinting is managed across the on-field rehab
221	 levels:
222	 Level 5: >95% up to 100%.
223	 Early sessions
224	 Structured progressions often use fixed distances (e.g., 60 m) with set completion
225	 times. For example:
226	 Reps gradually increase in speed across the session, building confidence and
227	 tolerance.
228	Sportsmith
229	  This method allows you to prescribe exact speeds, control intensity, and give
230	 athletes immediate feedback.
231	 Mid-stage sessions
232	 structures, such as broken strides:
233	 20 m acceleration 20 m speed maintenance 20 m deceleration.
234	 Completion times are set for the middle phase to ensure target velocities are
235	 reached.
236	 This balances controlled exposure with athlete feedback, using recovery walks and
237	 ongoing communication to manage comfort and confidence.
238	 Criteria for progression
239	 than simple tolerance. Objective criteria help guide decision-making:
240	 Biological healing time appropriate for the injury.
241	 Completion of previous running sessions with minimal pain or awareness.
242	 Force production benchmarks, such as:
243	 Nordics).
244	 Reactive strength assessments, such as hopping tasks, to ensure readiness for
245	 fast stretch-shortening cycle demands.
246	 Meeting these benchmarks provides confidence before exposing the athlete to high-
247	 velocity, high-risk tasks.
248	 Late-stage progression
249	 In the later stages, running speed is advanced using a combination of:
250	 Undulating approaches: Once above 85%, alternating sessions between higher
251	 and lower intensities to manage load and risk.
252	 of max before tapering slightly, while more complex injuries may require holding
253	 speeds or cycling intensity over several sessions.
254	 Crucially, athletes should achieve at least one, but ideally two, exposures above
255	 90% of max velocity before being cleared for training or competition.
256	Sportsmith
257	  Conclusion
258	 The progression from submaximal to maximal velocity running is a primary
259	 concern in on-field rehab. Each increase in speed brings greater intensity and
260	 mechanical demand, so athletes must be systematically prepared through
261	 preparatory drills, structured progressions, and objective readiness criteria. By
262	 combining linear and undulating approaches, and ensuring exposures above 90%
263	 are achieved, you can return athletes to competition with both confidence and
264	 resilience.
265	Sportsmith

338	 intuition alone.

344	 progressions that take athletes from controlled, low-risk movements to chaotic,
345	 sport-specific tasks at maximum intensity. Only when athletes can execute these
346	 actions confidently in unpredictable environments should they be considered ready
347	 for full return.

575	 Pulling it all
576	 together
577	 This course has explored the principles
578	 of rehab running and on-field
579	 rehabilitation for team sports. Across seven modules, we examined the key locomotive
580	 demands of invasion-based sports, the stages of on-field rehab, and the three major
581	 pillars:
582	 Submaximal and maximal velocity running.
583	 Multi-directional speed and agility.
584	 Sport-specific skills.
585	Sportsmith
586	  Each pillar was unpacked with clear strategies for progressing both intensity and
587	 complexity, supported by real-world case studies. The ultimate goal has been to
588	 help you build systematic, adaptable, and context-specific frameworks for guiding
589	 athletes safely back to competition.
590	 The core message
591	 No action in sport happens in isolation. Every sprint, deceleration, or cut occurs
592	 while the athlete is also making technical and tactical decisions. This means on-
593	 field rehab must integrate locomotive actions with game-relevant contexts. To do
594	 this effectively, practitioners need confidence that athletes have been exposed to
595	 both the demands of the actions themselves and the unpredictability of the
596	 environments in which they occur.
597	 Building your own framework
598	 If you want to design your own on-field rehab framework, four practical steps can
599	 guide you:
600	 1.Split your on-field rehab into levels.
601	 The number of levels (three, five, seven) is less important than having a
602	 clear structure that takes athletes from controlled reintroduction to chaotic,
603	 game-like environments.
604	 2.Identify your pillars.
605	 In this course, we used three: velocity running, multi-directional speed and
606	 agility, and sport-specific skills.
607	 You can adapt or expand these depending on your context and
608	 environment.
609	 3.Decide on your intensity factors.
610	 Choose the variables that will allow you to scale difficulty.
611	 Examples include running speed, change-of-direction angle, entry velocity,
612	 available space, reactivity demands, and practice structure (blocked
613	 serial random).
614	 4.Map your exercises and drills.
615	 Fit them into your chosen levels, pillars, and intensity factors.
616	 For example, early levels may use block practice and stationary drills, while
617	 later levels emphasize chaotic environments, positional skills, and
618	 competitive play.
619	 By following these four steps, you create a framework that is systematic yet flexible
620	 enough to adapt to different injuries, contexts, and athlete needs.
621	 A final perspective
622	 There is no single "right" or "wrong" way to deliver on-field rehab. The principles
623	 in this course are based on scientific evidence and years of applied practice, but
624	Sportsmith

626	 principles to your environment, your athletes, and the demands of your sport.
627	 If you remember one thing, let it be this: the two equally important objectives of
628	 on-field rehab are to progress the intensity of locomotive actions and to increase

630	 approach to these objectives will put you more than halfway toward a successful
631	 return-to-play outcome.

=========== PART 1 PDF
 COURSES
the
fundamentals
of on-field
rehabilitation
 Sportsmith
  Hi everybody,
 my name is Simon Harries.
 Thanks for joining us and I'm delighted to
 partner with Sportsmith to bring you this
 course where we are going to get into how I
 approach on-field rehab.
 The aim of this course is to give you the
 frameworks and tools to improve your on-
 field rehabilitation practices. To bring to life
 I will be presenting 3 in-depth case studies
 and allow you to see the commonalities
 across injuries
 Let's get going!
 Course introduction
 Rehab running, or on-field rehabilitation, is the crucial bridge between gym-based
 rehab and a full return to sport. Its purpose goes beyond healing the injured
 structure. It prepares the athlete to meet the technical, tactical, and physical
 demands of competition. This stage typically begins with the athlete's first steps
 back into running and progresses through increasingly complex and demanding
 scenarios. A structured framework ensures that the athlete regains locomotive and
 physical qualities while minimizing the risk of flare-ups or re-injury.
 On-field rehab has two primary objectives:
 Fully rehabilitating the injured area
 Preparing the athlete to handle the realities of their sport
 It is not enough to restore function in isolation. The athlete must also be
 conditioned to execute technical and tactical tasks under game-like intensity.
Sportsmith
  Managing risk is central to this process. Training loads must be progressed
 carefully to avoid negative responses such as soreness, tightness, or recurrence of
 the original injury. Success depends on clarity. You must know what physical and
 locomotive activities the athlete's sport demands and how to progress their ability
 to perform them safely and specifically.
 Finding common ground across team sports
 One of the biggest challenges in designing an on-field rehab framework is the sheer
 variety of actions performed in sport. Footballers dribble and press, rugby players
 tackle and pass, and basketball players cut and pivot. Yet, despite these surface
 differences, invasion-based sports all share the same tactical patterns: teams attack
 by creating and invading space, and they defend by protecting or closing space.
 Technical actions also overlap, such as carrying or passing a ball, pressing an
 opponent, or recovering into position.
 At the foundation of these tactical and technical actions lie a handful of locomotive
 tasks that never change. Sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, and changing
 direction are the common denominators of performance across team sports. These
 four actions form the locomotive pillars of on-field rehab. Regardless of the sport,
 you can build progression frameworks around these pillars and then layer technical
 or tactical context on top. For example, an acceleration drill may be progressed into
 a pressing scenario, while deceleration can be integrated into a defensive recovery
 pattern.
 Three pillars of on-field rehab
 All sound on-field rehab frameworks can be built around these three major themes:
 Submaximal and maximal velocity running
 Athletes must be gradually exposed to increasing speeds, culminating in repeated
 exposures at sprint velocity before they are ready to compete
 Multi-directional speed and agility
 Here, the athlete rehearses accelerations, decelerations, and changes of direction
 under increasing load, eventually re-creating the movement patterns required in
 offensive and defensive scenarios
 Sport-specific skills
 Technical and tactical tasks, passing, pressing, contesting, carrying must be layered
 onto locomotive drills so the athlete can demonstrate physical and skill execution
 together in realistic game contexts.
Sportsmith
  Putting the framework into practice
 The first step in applying these principles is to audit the sport in question. Break it
 down into technical, tactical, and physical domains, then identify the overlaps and
 commonalities. From there, anchor your framework on the four locomotive pillars;
 sprinting, acceleration, deceleration, and change of direction. Progression is about
 gradually increasing both the intensity and the complexity of tasks. Start with
 submaximal efforts and controlled environments, then move toward maximal
 outputs in chaotic, game-like contexts. Incorporate offensive and defensive
 scenarios so that physical tasks are performed for tactical purposes, such as creating
 space in attack or closing space in defense. Throughout the process, closely
 monitor the athlete's response. Signs of overload which are tightness, fatigue, or
 symptom recurrence should trigger an adjustment to the plan. Finally, use the
 athlete's competitive benchmarks as your guide. Re-exposure to sprint distance,
 high-speed running volumes, and repeated accelerations should all be achieved
 before the athlete is cleared for full return.
 Rehab running is far more than simply getting an athlete back to jogging. It is a
 structured, progressive, and context-driven process that reconnects the athlete with
 the locomotive, technical, and tactical demands of their sport. By grounding your
 framework in universal pillars, progressing tasks from simple to complex, and
 ensuring benchmarks are met, you can safely and effectively guide athletes from the
 gym back onto the field with confidence.
 Let's move onto part 2.
Sportsmith
=========== PART 2 PDF
 COURSES
 the
 fundamentals
 of on-field
 rehabilitation
 Part 2
 On-field rehab
 frameworks
 A framework is the backbone of
 on-field rehab. It provides structure,
 consistency, and efficiency, but it is not a rigid protocol. Instead, it acts as a guide that
 balances evidence with practitioner experience, allowing you to adapt to the needs of
 the individual athlete and the context of their injury. A good framework helps you
 manage risk, align rehab with the actual demands of sport, and make decisions quickly
 and confidently.
Sportsmith
  Why frameworks matter
 There are four key benefits to using a framework in on-field rehab. First, it allows
 you to take calculated risks. Rehab is never risk-free, but a framework acts like
 guardrails, ensuring you avoid progressing too quickly and causing a recurrence.
 Second, when a framework mirrors the performance requirements of sport, it
 enhances preparedness for return to play. Third, frameworks build in flexibility.
 They are not step-by-step manuals but adaptable guides that can be individualized
 for each athlete. And finally, they promote efficiency and consistency. With a
 structured approach, you can build programs faster, prescribe exercises with
 confidence, and make better decisions on the fly, all of which increase athlete trust
 in the process.
 Levels of on-field rehab
 On-field rehab can be split into levels that move progressively from controlled,
 low-intensity work to chaotic, high-intensity, game-like situations. These levels
 typically sit within the mid-to-late stages of rehab:
 Early stage: Gym-based work before progressing to the field.
 Mid-stage: Often broken into on-field rehab levels 1, 2, and 3.
 Late stage: Levels 4 and 5, leading into team training and return to play.
 For example, in the hamstring case study, the athlete completed one session at
 each level because of the injury's mild nature. With more severe injuries, multiple
 sessions at each level may be required. The athlete then transitioned into team
 training sessions before being cleared for competition.
 This level-based structure scaffolds the athlete's gradual exposure to the
 locomotive actions of their sport, ensuring intensity and complexity build
 systematically.
 Progressing intensity and complexity
 Two objectives drive the progression process: intensity and complexity.
 Intensity begins with competency. Athletes are reintroduced to locomotive
 actions, sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, changing direction, and
 submaximal running, at low to moderate speeds. Over time, the focus shifts to
 capacity, where the athlete must tolerate higher intensities and volumes until
 they can handle maximum velocity and repeated exposures.
 Complexity is best understood through the control-to-chaos continuum
 popularized by Matt Tabiner. Early sessions are highly controlled and low-risk.
 As athletes progress, the environment becomes less predictable, moving toward
 "chaos", highly reactive, game-like situations. Complexity is increased by
 manipulating variables such as space, opposition, and task constraints, creating
 more realistic environments for decision-making and movement execution.
Sportsmith
  A common misconception is that each new level automatically means more chaos
 across all drills. In reality, progression is gradual. Some actions may still require
 controlled environments at higher intensities, while others are ready to be tested
 under chaotic, game-like conditions. Intensity and complexity must be treated as
 separate but equally important goals.
 Control to chaos in practice
 The continuum is not simply about intensity or randomness, it is about preparing
 athletes to act effectively under the same uncertainty they will face in competition.
 At the controlled end, you structure the environment tightly, focusing on safe
 reintroduction of movement. At the chaotic end, drills replicate unpredictable
 scenarios where athletes must choose and execute the right action under pressure.
 This progression demands careful design. Using constraint-based learning
 principles, you can manipulate the task, the environment, or the individual's role to
 adjust the level of complexity. Over time, the ratio shifts: more work is performed
 in chaotic settings while less remains in tightly controlled conditions.
 End-stage rehab: competitive demands
 At the end of the process, athletes must be able to combine high intensity with high
 complexity. This is not just about physical readiness but also about confidence and
 decision-making. An athlete should be willing to sprint into space, accelerate to
 chase down an opponent, or react decisively in a chaotic small-sided game. If they
 hesitate in these competitive situations, they are not ready to return.
 In other words, the final stage of rehab is not optional chaos, it is essential.
 Exposing athletes to competitive, high-risk, and high-intensity scenarios is the only
 way to ensure they are prepared for the realities of their sport.
 Conclusion
 Frameworks bring order to the messy reality of on-field rehab. By breaking the
 process into progressive levels and systematically increasing both intensity and
 complexity, you create a safe and effective pathway back to competition. The
 ultimate goal is simple: an athlete who is physically prepared, mentally confident,
 and capable of executing high-intensity actions in chaotic, competitive
 environments. Anything less leaves them underprepared for the demands of sport.
Sportsmith
=========== PART 3 PDF
 COURSES
 the
 fundamentals
 of on-field
 rehabilitation
 Part 3
 Linear submaximal &
 maximal running
 progressions
 The first major pillar of on-field rehab
 is the progression from submaximal to
 maximal running velocity. This pillar begins with preparing the athlete to return to
 running and continues through jogging, running, striding, and ultimately sprinting.
 Each step involves increasing intensity and mechanical demand, so a structured and
 careful progression is essential.
Sportsmith
  Understanding running velocities
 Running speed categories can be broken down into clear ranges:
 Walking: <6 km/h, less than 25% of max velocity.
 Sprinting: >27 km/h, above 85% of max velocity.
 As speed increases, vertical ground reaction forces grow larger, contact times get
 shorter, and muscular power demands rise--especially at the hip, knee, and ankle.
 This has implications for injury-specific rehab: ankle-dominant strategies are more
 relevant at lower speeds, while hip-dominant mechanics dominate as athletes
 approach striding and sprinting.
 Preparation for running
 Before progressing into steady-state running, athletes should demonstrate
 competence in drills that reintroduce upright running mechanics and repetitive
 impact cycles. These include:
 Dribble walks and runs (over ankle, shin, and knee height) to reinforce front-
 side mechanics.
 Skipping drills (e.g., A-skips) to add stiffness and reactivity.
 Low-intensity jumping such as pogos and unilateral hops for repetitive loading.
 Scissor shuffles and bounds to target aggressive hip flexion and extension.
 These preparatory drills serve both as warm-ups and readiness assessments,
 ensuring athletes can tolerate dynamic impact and postural demands before
 progressing.
 Progressing running speed
 The transition from jogging to sprinting is managed across the on-field rehab
 levels:
 Level 5: >95% up to 100%.
 Early sessions
 Structured progressions often use fixed distances (e.g., 60 m) with set completion
 times. For example:
 Reps gradually increase in speed across the session, building confidence and
 tolerance.
Sportsmith
  This method allows you to prescribe exact speeds, control intensity, and give
 athletes immediate feedback.
 Mid-stage sessions
 structures, such as broken strides:
 20 m acceleration 20 m speed maintenance 20 m deceleration.
 Completion times are set for the middle phase to ensure target velocities are
 reached.
 This balances controlled exposure with athlete feedback, using recovery walks and
 ongoing communication to manage comfort and confidence.
 Criteria for progression
 than simple tolerance. Objective criteria help guide decision-making:
 Biological healing time appropriate for the injury.
 Completion of previous running sessions with minimal pain or awareness.
 Force production benchmarks, such as:
 Nordics).
 Reactive strength assessments, such as hopping tasks, to ensure readiness for
 fast stretch-shortening cycle demands.
 Meeting these benchmarks provides confidence before exposing the athlete to high-
 velocity, high-risk tasks.
 Late-stage progression
 In the later stages, running speed is advanced using a combination of:
 Undulating approaches: Once above 85%, alternating sessions between higher
 and lower intensities to manage load and risk.
 of max before tapering slightly, while more complex injuries may require holding
 speeds or cycling intensity over several sessions.
 Crucially, athletes should achieve at least one, but ideally two, exposures above
 90% of max velocity before being cleared for training or competition.
Sportsmith
  Conclusion
 The progression from submaximal to maximal velocity running is a primary
 concern in on-field rehab. Each increase in speed brings greater intensity and
 mechanical demand, so athletes must be systematically prepared through
 preparatory drills, structured progressions, and objective readiness criteria. By
 combining linear and undulating approaches, and ensuring exposures above 90%
 are achieved, you can return athletes to competition with both confidence and
 resilience.

 Part 4
 Multidirectional
 speed & agility
 progressions
 Multi-directional speed and agility is a
 broad umbrella term that describes an
 athlete's ability to accelerate, decelerate, change direction, and maintain speed in
 multiple movement patterns. Unlike agility in its narrow sense, which is often defined
 by cognitive and perceptual elements, multi-directional speed incorporates both the
 physical and decision-making aspects needed in sport. It is central to on-field rehab
 because these high-intensity locomotive actions occur constantly in invasion-based
 games.
Sportsmith
  Breaking Down Multi-Directional Speed
 Multi-directional speed can be separated into three key components:
 Acceleration (short, explosive starts).
 Deceleration (rapid braking under load).
 Change of direction (angles ranging from shallow cuts to 180-degree turns).
 All three involve high rates of velocity change, which demand large ground reaction
 forces, rapid eccentric braking, and robust technical execution. This makes them
 both essential to performance and high risk if progressed poorly.
 What influences intensity?
 The intensity of multi-directional speed actions can be manipulated through
 several key variables:
 higher demands.
 direction loads.
 than shallow ones.
 time raises joint stress.
 intensity.
 competitive scenarios.
 These factors rarely operate independently. For example, higher approach speeds
 also raise the eccentric braking demand of a cut, while reducing space naturally
 lowers approach velocity. Thinking about them in combination helps you design
 drills that match both the athlete's current capacity and the desired rehab outcome.
 Linking intensity and complexity
 Just as with straight-line running, two main objectives guide progression in multi-
 directional work:
 Drills can be plotted on a matrix of intensity (vertical axis) and complexity
 (horizontal axis). Early rehab drills sit low on both, while later-stage drills push
 into high intensity and high complexity. This interplay aligns with the broader on-
 field rehab process: athletes must redevelop locomotive actions and then
 demonstrate them in chaotic environments.
Sportsmith
  Practical drill progressions
 Using the hamstring case study as a reference, here's how drills might be
