# RTP_Constraints_Course

A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).

**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
phase of return to performance in American football.

## How to work here

Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.

Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |
| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |
| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. 0001 written 2026-09-03 (opposed vs unopposed). |
| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. |
| `reference/gray-infographics/` | Local copies of Rob Gray's free infographics, saved 2026-09-03 because the site is one person's. Includes the 21-study comparative table, extracted and searchable. **Do not republish, do not commit.** See its `README.md`. |
| `sources/` | Full-text books and long PDFs obtained legitimately. Author-supplied — **never redistribute, never commit.** Holds the Myszka book (240 pages, printed 14–253), its OCR text sidecar, the reversible scan manifest, and the extracted bibliography. |
| `scripts/` | `velocity_band_sheet.py` builds the Baylor velocity-band sheet (Harries' levels from GPS; writes to Drive only, since it names athletes). Also the book-scan pipeline. `scan_pipeline.py` turns phone photos into a page-ordered OCR'd PDF and **refuses to rename unless the arithmetic gate passes**; `verify_pdf.py` proves page order afterwards by an independent route. Read `scan_pipeline.py`'s docstring before the next scanning job — it carries every trap found so far. |
| `docs/handoffs/` | Durable cross-session handoffs. Newest first. |
| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. 0001 records the lesson-0001 hook decision and Joe's starting floor. |

## Rules specific to this workspace

- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.
- **Every lesson ends in something Joe could do at practice tomorrow.**
- `GLOSSARY.md` does not exist yet by design — see `NOTES.md`.
- **Phase 2 is a drill-design tool.** Do not start it until the lessons have specified it.
  Route: `/grill-with-docs` → `/prototype` → `/implement`. Local-only per Baylor IT.

## Source library

Papers referenced as `LIB/…` live in `~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/research-papers/`.
Search with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`. Zotero MCP was down on 2026-09-01.

The user has asked you to teach them something. This is a stateful request - they intend to learn the topic over multiple sessions.

## Teaching Workspace

Treat the current directory as a teaching workspace. The state of their learning is captured in this directory in several files:

- `MISSION.md`: A document capturing the _reason_ the user is interested in the topic. This should be used to ground all teaching. Use the format in [MISSION-FORMAT.md](./MISSION-FORMAT.md).
- `./reference/*.html`: A directory of reference materials. These are the compressed learnings from the lessons - cheat sheets, reference algorithms, syntax, yoga poses, glossaries. They are the raw units of learning. They should be beautiful documents which print out well, and are designed for quick reference.
- `RESOURCES.md`: A list of resources which can be explored to ground your teaching in contextual knowledge, or to acquire knowledge and wisdom. Use the format in [RESOURCES-FORMAT.md](./RESOURCES-FORMAT.md).
- `./learning-records/*.md`: A directory of learning records, which capture what the user has learned. These are loosely equivalent to architectural decision records in software development - they capture non-obvious lessons and key insights that may need to be revised later, or drive future sessions. These should be used to calculate the zone of proximal development. They are titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.md`, where the number increments each time. Use the format in [LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md](./LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md).
- `./lessons/*.html`: A directory of lessons. A **lesson** is a single, self-contained HTML output that teaches one tightly-scoped thing tied to the mission. This is the primary unit of teaching in this workspace.
- `./assets/*`: Reusable **components** shared across lessons. See [Assets](#assets).
- `NOTES.md`: A scratchpad for you to jot down user preferences, or working notes.

## Philosophy

To learn at a deep level, the user needs three things:

- **Knowledge**, captured from high-quality, high-trust resources
- **Skills**, acquired through highly-relevant interactive lessons devised by you, based on the knowledge
- **Wisdom**, which comes from interacting with other learners and practitioners

Before the `RESOURCES.md` is well-populated, your focus should be to find high-quality resources which will help the user acquire knowledge. Never trust your parametric knowledge.

Some topics may require more skills than knowledge. Learning more about theoretical physics might be more knowledge-based. For yoga, more skills-based.

### Fluency vs Storage Strength

You should be careful to split between two types of learning:

- **Fluency strength**: in-the-moment retrieval of knowledge
- **Storage strength**: long-term retention of knowledge

Fluency can give the user an illusory sense of mastery, but storage strength is the real goal. Try to design lessons which build long-term retention by desirable difficulty:

- Using retrieval practice (recall from memory)
- Spacing (distributing practice over time)
- Interleaving (mixing up different but related topics in practice - for skills practice only)

## Lessons

A lesson is the main thing you produce: the unit in which knowledge and skills reach the user. Each lesson is one self-contained HTML file, saved to `./lessons/` and titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.html` where the number increments each time.

A lesson should be **beautiful**, with clean, readable typography and layout, since the user will return to these later to review. Think Tufte.

The lesson should be short, and completable very quickly. Learners' working memory is very small, and we need to stay within it. But each lesson should give the user a single tangible win that they can build on. It should be directly tied to the mission, and should be in the user's zone of proximal development.

If possible, open the lesson file for the user by running a CLI command.

Each lesson should link via HTML anchors to other lessons and reference documents.

Each lesson should recommend a primary source for the user to read or watch. This should be the most high-quality, high-trust resource you found on the topic.

Each lesson should contain a reminder to ask followup questions to the agent. The agent is their teacher, and can assist with anything that's unclear.

## Assets

Lessons are built from reusable **components**, stored in `./assets/`: stylesheets, quiz widgets, simulators, diagram helpers, and anything else a second lesson could reuse.

Reuse is the default, not the exception. Before authoring a lesson, read `./assets/` and build from the components already there. When a lesson needs something new and reusable, write it as a component in `./assets/` and link to it; never inline code a future lesson would duplicate.

A shared stylesheet is the first component every workspace earns: every lesson links it, so the lessons look like one consistent course rather than a pile of one-offs. As the workspace grows, so should the component library.

## The Mission

Every lesson should be tied into the mission - the reason that the user is interested in learning about the topic.

If the user is unclear about the mission, or the `MISSION.md` is not populated, your first job should be to question the user on why they want to learn this.

Failing to understand the mission will mean knowledge acquisition is not grounded in real-world goals. Lessons will feel too abstract. You will have no way of judging what the user should do next.

Missions may change as the user develops more skills and knowledge. This is normal - make sure to update the `MISSION.md` and add a learning record to capture the change. Confirm with the user before changing the mission.

## Zone Of Proximal Development

Each lesson, the user should always feel as if they are being challenged 'just enough'.

The user may specify an exact thing they want to learn. If they don't, figure out their zone of proximal development by:

- Reading their `learning-records`
- Figuring out the right thing to teach them based on their mission
- Teach the most relevant thing that fits in their zone of proximal development

## Knowledge

Lessons should be designed around a skill the user is going to learn. The knowledge in the lesson should be only what's required to acquire that skill. You teach the knowledge first, then get the user to practice the skills via an interactive feedback loop.

Knowledge should first be gathered from trusted resources. Use `RESOURCES.md` to keep track of them. Lessons should be littered with citations - links to external resources to back up any claim made. This increases the trustworthiness of the lesson.

For acquiring knowledge, difficulty is the enemy. It eats working memory you need for understanding.

## Skills

If knowledge is all about acquisition, skills are about durability and flexibility. Make the knowledge stick.

For skill acquisition, difficulty is the tool. Effortful retrieval is what builds storage strength. Skills should be taught through interactive lessons. There are several tools at your disposal:

- Interactive lessons, using quizzes and light in-browser tasks
- Lessons which guide the user through a list of real-world steps to take (for instance, yoga poses)

Each of these should be based on a **feedback loop**, where the user receives feedback on their performance. This feedback loop should be as tight as possible, giving feedback immediately - and ideally automatically.

For quizzes, each answer should be exactly the same number of words (and characters, if possible). Don't give the user any clues about the answer through formatting.

## Acquiring Wisdom

Wisdom comes from true real-world interaction - testing your skills outside the learning environment.

When the user asks a question that appears to require wisdom, your default posture should be to attempt to answer - but to ultimately delegate to a **community**.

A community is a place (online or offline) where the user can test their skills in the real world. This might be a forum, a subreddit, a real-world class (budget permitting) or a local interest group.

You should attempt to find high-reputation communities the user can join. If the user expresses a preference that they don't want to join a community, respect it.

## Reference Documents

While creating lessons, you should also create reference documents. Lessons can reference these documents - they are useful for tracking raw units of knowledge useful across lessons.

Lessons will rarely be revisited later - reference documents will be. They should be the compressed essence of the lesson, in a format designed for quick reference.

Some learning topics lend themselves to reference:

- Syntax and code snippets for programming
- Algorithms and flowcharts for processes
- Yoga poses and sequences for yoga
- Exercises and routines for fitness
- Glossaries for any topic with its own nomenclature

Glossaries, in particular, are an essential reference. Once one is created, it should be adhered to in every lesson.

## `NOTES.md`

The user will sometimes express preferences of how they want to be taught, or things you should keep in mind. This is the place to record those preferences, so you can refer back to them when designing lessons or working with the user.

Constraints-led return to performance · Lesson 0001

The drill that hid the deficit

Why a drill with no opponent cannot tell you an athlete is ready, what the opponent actually adds, and one sentence you can say to someone who was not there.

About 40 minutes the way you work: read once, take notes, do the quiz, then plan the field task.
Grounded in MISSION.md and the key-answers digest of your 3 September interview. Cheat sheet: reference/0001-opposed-vs-unopposed.

1. Start with a case you already own

In the interview you described a returning offensive lineman with a target game. You ran a needs assessment, worked a reverse calendar back from the game, and built run-blocking days, pass-blocking days and a reaction day. That method stays.

Then this happened. In the non-reactive drills he looked strong. He was experienced enough to time them up. In the reactive pass drills his performance dropped and he reported more strain. And at the end you could not load him at your own size, so a position coach and real defensive-line bodies had to finish the job.

You made a constraints argument without the vocabulary for it. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, one peer-reviewed paper to stand on, and a sentence you can say to a physician or a coordinator who was not at practice.

The belief this lesson corrects

“He looked clean in the pre-set pass drill, so he is ready.” A clean rep in a drill with no opponent shows he can execute a plan he already knows. It does not show he can play football.

2. What the opponent is: information

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan and Otte (2025) put it in one line borrowed from Gibson: behavior affords behavior. How the other person moves is what shapes what the athlete can do next. In contact and invasion sports, the most useful information is tied to another body: the distance between them, his posture, how fast the gap is closing.

Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., O Sullivan, M., & Otte, F. (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. Quest, 1–21. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759 — pp. 6–7. The Gibson line is The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), p. 135, as quoted there.

Now put that on a pass set. The lineman’s job is to pick up the rusher’s first step, his lean, the closing distance, and to set and re-anchor against it as it changes. Take the rusher away and there is nothing to pick up. The lineman sets to a plan instead. He can time it. That is why he looked strong. The drill did not lie to you. It just could not measure the thing you needed to know.

Parry and colleagues say it plainly: if opponents are not present, athletes “will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals” (p. 6). What is missing from the unopposed drill is not effort or load. It is the information the job runs on.

3. Two words, and two ways to make a drill easier

Unopposed practice isolates a skill and repeats it with no opponent present. Opposed practice keeps an opponent in the task, so the problem is alive: it changes moment to moment, it differs each time, and it cannot be fully predicted (Parry et al., 2025, pp. 2, 6). Those two words are the first glossary candidates in this course. Use them at practice this week.

Here is the part that changes how you regress a drill. There are two ways to make a task easier, and they are not the same.

MoveWhat you doWhat happens to the information
DecomposeTake a piece out. No rusher. Bag instead of a body. Cones instead of a defender.Gone. The athlete solves a different, smaller problem.
SimplifyKeep the whole problem. Turn the pressure down. Rusher at half speed, hands behind his back, scripted first step.Still there. The athlete solves the real problem at a lower level.

Parry and colleagues give the second move directly: opposition “can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success” (p. 4). Rob Gray draws the same line between the two schools of coaching, decomposition on one side and simplification on the other; his table of comparative studies lists one head-to-head in volleyball where simplification beat decomposition. Treat that row as a pointer, not a citation, until the paper has been read.

Gray, R. Two Approaches and Comparative Training Studies infographics, perceptionaction.com. Local copies: two-approaches.md (last row) and comparative-training-studies.md (study 17, Caldeira et al. 2023, volleyball). The comparative table is the page to bring when someone pushes back.
This course’s extension, not the paper’s

In return to performance the reflex regression is to strip the drill to no opponent. On the logic above that does not simplify the task. It deletes it, and it deletes exactly the perception the returning athlete has to rebuild. Parry et al. write about skill development, not rehabilitation. Applying it to return to performance is our step, and you should say so when you cite it.

4. What the paper does not say

It does not say “never unopposed.” Read it fairly, because the first physician who has read it will.

  • Unopposed work has a place as exploration: a chance to search many ways of moving with little consequence, not to perfect one technique by repetition (pp. 3–6).
  • Unopposed drills can be made alive by putting other moving bodies in the same space, even when nobody is defending anyone (pp. 4–5).
  • There is “limited evidence to suggest that unopposed practice must precede opposed, game-like practice” (p. 6). The ladder you were taught is a habit, not a finding.

So the claim you can defend is narrower and stronger than “opposed is better.” It is this: an unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, because the information the athlete times up is the information that is missing. Use unopposed work to build capacity and to explore. Do not use it to prove anything.

No opponentBodies in the spaceOpponent, pressure downLive opponent

Readiness lives on the right half of that bar. Regress along it. Do not jump off it.

5. Football, on tape

The course’s anchor paper has the closest case to yours. Yearby, Myszka, Roberts, Woods and Davids (2024) worked with an NFL defensive end in the off-season. Instead of unopposed pass-rush technique, the task kept a centre, an offensive tackle and a quarterback on the field, so the rusher had to couple his movement to the snap and to the tackle’s set (p. 15). Over the off-season they saw new options emerge: an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, hand-chop variations (p. 18). Nobody taught those moves. The opponent did.

Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. Free full text: Sheffield Hallam repository. Case observations, not a controlled trial.

Parry and colleagues do the same for running backs (pp. 11–16). You made a constraints argument without the vocabulary for it. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, one peer-reviewed paper to stand on, and a sentence you can say to a physician or a coordinator who was not at practice.

“He looked clean in the pre-set pass drill, so he is ready.” A clean rep in a drill with no opponent shows he can execute a plan he already knows. It does not show he can play football.

200:**Status change: Emergence was filed under Wisdom as a community. It is also a free, on-mission written source, and it is the only place found so far where the ecological-dynamics people write directly about injured people.** Run by **Shawn Myszka and Tyler Yearby** — two of the four practitioners and two of the three textbook authors. [Blog index](https://emergentmvmt.com/emergence-blog/)
206:- **["Ecological Dynamics in Musculoskeletal Rehab"](https://emergentmvmt.com/ecological-dynamics-in-musculoskeletal-rehab/)** (May 2024) — **Part 1; author unresolved, see warning above.** The argument against tissue-focused rehab. **The idea worth stealing: pain and injury are *organism constraints*.** Reduced range, weakness, fear, low self-efficacy and narrowed attention all shrink the athlete's **"field of affordances"** — the set of actions they can even perceive as available. His worked contrast: a rested powerlifter and a fatigued person with back pain look at the same box and perceive different possibilities. **This gives Joe a single mechanism that ties the medical facts to the performance problem.** Cites Gibson (1979), Bernstein (1996), Stilwell & Harman (2019), Vaz et al. (2023).
209:- **["Injury and Affordance Perception"](https://emergentmvmt.com/injury-and-affordance-perception/)** (Apr 2023) — by **Javier Miler-Estrada** — **one "l", per the site's own byline and bio, verified 2026-09-02. The Transforming Basketball podcast bills him "Javier Miller-Estrada" with two. Use the Emergence spelling; flag the variant if he is ever contacted.** Co-founder of Ignite Performance (Chandler, AZ). **The closest thing found to a written RTP progression in this tradition**, and it ends in an **ACL case study of a football player** moving from facility work to field sessions against real opponents. 217:Checked 2026-09-02, because "Rob Gray" is easy to file as a generic ecological-dynamics name. **He is not that. He is an experimental psychologist (PhD), Associate Professor at ASU, with a top paper near 900 citations** — the most rigorously credentialed of the four practitioners. **But his research base is attention, choking under pressure, virtual-reality transfer and baseball batting — not rehabilitation.** Most-cited: attention and choking in complex skill (2004), focus of attention in baseball batting (2007), transfer from virtual to real batting (2017).
221:- **Gray, R. (2015).** Differences in Attentional Focus Associated With Recovery From Sports Injury: Does Injury Induce an Internal Focus? *Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 37*(6), 607–616. [PubMed 26866768](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26866768/) · [Human Kinetics](https://journals.humankinetics.com/view/journals/jsep/37/6/article-p607.xml)
222:  **This is Gray's one injury paper, it is peer-reviewed, and it supplies the mechanism the whole course has been missing.** Baseball players recovering from knee or elbow surgery were tested against expert and novice controls. **Injured athletes had an internal focus of attention localised on the injured area, and batted significantly worse than expert controls.** In other words: **injury is associated with an attentional habit that degrades performance.** *(Worded carefully — this is a between-groups comparison and Gray's own title poses it as a question. 262:**Recommendation:** take all eight free guides now; buy *How We Learn to Move*; **join the CLA certification waitlist only if Joe's development budget is real** — $1,995 buys direct feedback from the textbook's co-author, which nothing else in this file offers, but the free material plus the Emergence blog covers most of the same ground at zero cost.
327:**Why he thinks it works:** the CLA already contains the other methods — it is **implicit learning**, it produces an **external focus of attention** by default, and combined with **representative learning design** it is *"optimally designed for transfer of training."* **That single sentence connects it to the attentional-focus thread above.**

217:Checked 2026-09-02, because "Rob Gray" is easy to file as a generic ecological-dynamics name. **He is not that. He is an experimental psychologist (PhD), Associate Professor at ASU, with a top paper near 900 citations** — the most rigorously credentialed of the four practitioners. **But his research base is attention, choking under pressure, virtual-reality transfer and baseball batting — not rehabilitation.** Most-cited: attention and choking in complex skill (2004), focus of attention in baseball batting (2007), transfer from virtual to real batting (2017).
221:- **Gray, R. (2015).** Differences in Attentional Focus Associated With Recovery From Sports Injury: Does Injury Induce an Internal Focus? *Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 37*(6), 607–616. [PubMed 26866768](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26866768/) · [Human Kinetics](https://journals.humankinetics.com/view/journals/jsep/37/6/article-p607.xml)
222:  **This is Gray's one injury paper, it is peer-reviewed, and it supplies the mechanism the whole course has been missing.** Baseball players recovering from knee or elbow surgery were tested against expert and novice controls. **Injured athletes had an internal focus of attention localised on the injured area, and batted significantly worse than expert controls.** In other words: **injury is associated with an attentional habit that degrades performance.** *(Worded carefully — this is a between-groups comparison and Gray's own title poses it as a question. The causal story is carried by the chain, not this paper alone.)* That explains the athlete who passes every physical test and still does not play like himself — **and it is a performance problem, not a strength problem, so it is Joe's to solve.** **Acquire this next, ahead of the PMC12649574 paper already flagged above.**
262:**Recommendation:** take all eight free guides now; buy *How We Learn to Move*; **join the CLA certification waitlist only if Joe's development budget is real** — $1,995 buys direct feedback from the textbook's co-author, which nothing else in this file offers, but the free material plus the Emergence blog covers most of the same ground at zero cost.
327:**Why he thinks it works:** the CLA already contains the other methods — it is **implicit learning**, it produces an **external focus of attention** by default, and combined with **representative learning design** it is *"optimally designed for transfer of training."* **That single sentence connects it to the attentional-focus thread above.**
391:**5. Where he concedes the clinician's ground — quote this in a medical meeting.** Gray is explicit that ecological coaches do **not** simply stand back: *"we're guiding self-organization, we're not just standing back and letting athletes do anything."* Solutions must carry certain **invariant properties**, and he names **a movement pattern that might cause injury** as a legitimate reason to intervene. **This is the sentence that makes the approach defensible to a physician**, and it matches Yearby's principle 5 on the Emergence blog.
403:### One worked lesson thread: attentional focus
409:1. **Gray (2015)** — injury is associated with an internal focus on the injured part, and worse performance. *(Not owned; acquire.)*
410:2. **Miler-Estrada, Emergence blog** — anxiety makes the athlete underestimate what they can do, shrinking perceived affordances. *(Free, above.)*
411:3. **Singh, Gokeler & Benjaminse (2021)** — attentional-focus strategies after ACL reconstruction (`EYKZD68B`, Tier 2 below). *(Owned.)*
456:- **Singh, H., Gokeler, A., & Benjaminse, A. (2021).** Effective Attentional Focus Strategies after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Commentary. *IJSPT*. [doi:10.26603/001c.29848](https://doi.org/10.26603/001c.29848) · `key=EYKZD68B`
464:Twenty `ground` queries across the whole library (constraints-led, ecological dynamics, affordances, representative design, self-organisation, nonlinear pedagogy, perception-action, dynamical systems, variability of practice, differential learning, external focus, degeneracy, attunement, small-sided games, transfer, and more). **71 unique items matched; 16 were already listed above. These are the ones worth adding.**
477:  **Harjiv Singh's fourth appearance in this file.** OPTIMAL Theory (Wulf & Lewthwaite) — external focus, autonomy support, enhanced expectancies. **Not the same theory as ecological dynamics, and that is exactly why to teach it:** it is the strongest neighbouring account of the same phenomena, and it slots straight into the attentional-focus thread above. **Joe should know where the two frameworks agree and where they do not.**
507:- **Emergence** (Myszka & Yearby) — courses, mentorship, and a practitioner community explicitly built on movement-skill acquisition in football. **Reviewed 2026-09-02: it is also a free written knowledge source, including three posts on the rehab seam and Yearby's own plain-language framework — see the Emergence blog section above.** It also runs the **CSAS** credential, which is a career lever for Joe, and the Adaptable Athlete Podcast.
516:2. **OPEN, and wider than first recorded — there is almost no Rob Gray in the library at all.** A `ground` sweep on 2026-09-02 found him only in passing mentions; **not one stored item has him as an author.** He is the most rigorously credentialed of the four practitioners (PhD experimental psychology, ASU, ~900 citations on his top paper), so this is a real hole. **Priority order to fix it: (a) Gray (2015) on injury and internal attentional focus — peer-reviewed, and the mechanism the course needs, see the Rob Gray section above; (b) *How We Learn to Move*, still the best plain-language on-ramp for a clinician.**

Differences in Attentional Focus Associated With Recovery From Sports Injury: Does Injury Induce an Internal Focus?
Gray R. Journal of sport & exercise psychology 2015
Although it is commonly believed that focusing too much attention on the injured body area impairs recovery in sports, this has not been directly assessed. The present study investigated attentional focus following sports injury. Experienced baseball position players recovering from knee surgery (Expt 1) and baseball pitchers recovering from elbow surgery (Expt 2) performed simulated batting and pitching respectively. They also performed three different secondary tasks: leg angle judgments, arm angle judgments, and judgments about the ball leaving their bat/hand. Injured athletes were compared with expert and novice control groups. Performance on the secondary tasks indicated that the injured batters had an internal focus of attention localized on the area of the injury resulting in significantly poorer batting performance as compared with the expert controls. Injured pitchers had a diffuse, internal attentional focus similar to that of novices resulting in poorer pitching performance as compared with the expert controls.

### CONSIDERING AN EXTERNAL FOCUS OF ATTENTION TO OPTIMIZE MOVEMENT OUTCOME (1)

## CONSIDERING AN EXTERNAL FOCUS OF ATTENTION TO OPTIMIZE MOVEMENT OUTCOME

A subtle change in the wording of exercise instruction prior to movement execution can promote an external focus of attention so that attention is directed to one’s intended effect of the movement (goal-directed attention), in contrast to paying attention to one’s own body movements (i.e., internal focus of attention or self-directed attention). This external focus of attention centers on the ability to engage both the perceptual-cognitive and physical performance factors in the functional task environment.23 For example, in an effort to improve balance performance, a patient may perform a single leg balance task on a Bosu ball (BOSU, Ashland, OH). A clinician may instruct the patient using an internal focus of attention such as, “minimize movement of the feet”. However, by just changing one word to “minimize movement of the Bosu” the instructions become externally focused. In addition, an external focus of attention can also be elicited by means of a metaphor (e.g., “stand still like you are stuck on Velcro”), analogy ("imagine you are on the peak of a mountain, stay on the mountain!), an object attached to the body (“keep the tape attached to the chest still”), or an imagined object, where a mental image of the movement goal is obtained (e.g., thinking of the leg as a line, “keep the line straight”).24–28

### INTRODUCTION

## INTRODUCTION

A rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is one of the most common sport related injuries. Patients who want to continue to pursue pivoting type of sports often undergo ACL reconstruction (ACLR) followed by extensive periods of rehabilitation. However, patients after ACLR still may have up to a 40 times greater risk of reinjury relative to those without injury.1 Following ACLR, aberrant movement patterns have been linked to an increased risk of a second ACL injury and may also explain why not all patients return to their pre-injury level.2–4 Current rehabilitation approaches may not optimally target deficits in motor control. ### Abstract

## Abstract

Individuals after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) have a high rate of reinjury upon return to competitive sports. Deficits in motor control may influence reinjury risk and can be addressed during rehabilitation with motor learning strategies. When instructing patients in performing motor tasks after ACLR, an external focus of attention directed to the intended movement effect has been shown to be more effective in reducing reinjury risk than an internal focus of attention on body movements. While this concept is mostly agreed upon, recent literature has made it clear that the interpretation and implementation of an external focus of attention within ACLR rehabilitation needs to be better described. The purpose of this commentary is to provide a clinical framework for the application of attentional focus strategies and guide clinicians towards effectively utilizing an external focus of attention in rehabilitation after ACLR.

Constraints-led return to performance · Reference

Opposed vs unopposed

One page. The residue of lesson 0001.

Two words

TermMeaning
UnopposedA skill isolated and repeated with no opponent present. Good for exploring and for capacity. Not evidence of readiness.
OpposedAn opponent stays in the task. The problem is alive: it changes, it varies, it cannot be fully predicted.

The claim you can defend

An unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, because the information the athlete times up is exactly the information that is missing. Football runs on reading another body: distance, posture, closing speed.

Two ways to make a drill easier

MoveDoInformation
DecomposeRemove the opponent. Bag, cones, air.Deleted
SimplifyKeep the opponent. Half speed. Hands behind back. Scripted start, live finish.Kept

Regress by simplifying. In return to performance, stripping to no opponent is this course’s named trap, not a finding from the paper.

The ladder

No opponentBodies in the spaceOpponent, pressure downLive opponent

Readiness is measured on the right half. Move along the bar. Do not jump off it.

Who plays the opponent

  1. Pair two position groups. Both get a live problem.
  2. Same position, other side of the ball.
  3. A coach. Less skilled, still alive.

You cannot load a lineman at your own size. Step one is the right call, and it has a citation.

Three questions of any drill used as evidence

  1. What information did he have to pick up?
  2. What did he have to do with it?
  3. How much pressure was it under?

If the answer to question one is “nothing,” the drill is not evidence.

The sentence

“He had to read [information] and [action] with the opponent at [pressure]. He did that in [n] of [N] reps. The unopposed drill could not show me that, because there was nothing in it to read.”

Sources

Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., O Sullivan, M., & Otte, F. (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice. Quest. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759. Zotero CA2CRR6Z. Argument pp. 3–7; football case pp. 11–16; who plays the opponent p. 15.
Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. Free: Sheffield Hallam. Defensive-end case p. 15, observations p. 18.
Sarama, A., interviewed by R. Gray. Perception & Action Podcast ep. 489. “Scripted start, live finish.” Practitioner opinion.
Gray, R. Comparative Training Studies table, local copy at gray-infographics/comparative-training-studies.md. The page to bring when someone pushes back.

Constraints-led return to performance · Lesson 0002

Attention goes where you point it

Why an athlete can pass every test and still not play like himself, what injury does to where he looks, and two ways to move his attention off the knee and onto the game: the words you use, and the drill you build.

About 35 minutes the way you work: read once, take notes, do the quiz, then plan the field task.
Builds on lesson 0001. Grounded in MISSION.md. Cheat sheet: reference/0002-attentional-focus.

0. From last time, before you read on

Answer from memory. Retrieving it now is what makes it stick; rereading does not.

Why can an unopposed drill not prove a returning athlete is ready?

If you ran the lesson 0001 field task, have your two written lines next to you. You will use them in section 7.

1. The athlete who tests fine and plays wrong

You know this athlete. The strength numbers are back. He has hit his running targets. He is cleared. And in team drills he is a half-step late, he hesitates before the plant, and he does not look like himself. The physical tests say he is ready. Your eyes say he is not. That is exactly the subjective call you told us you struggle to defend.

There is a peer-reviewed study of this athlete. Rob Gray (2015) tested experienced baseball players who were recovering from surgery: position players after knee surgery batting in a simulator, and pitchers after elbow surgery. He compared them with healthy expert players and with novices. While they batted or pitched, they also made quick side judgements, about the angle of their leg, the angle of their arm, or the ball leaving the bat. The side judgements show where their attention was.

The injured batters “had an internal focus of attention localized on the area of the injury,” and they batted “significantly poorer” than the healthy experts. The injured pitchers had a scattered, internal focus “similar to that of novices,” and they also pitched worse.

Gray, R. (2015). Differences in attentional focus associated with recovery from sports injury: Does injury induce an internal focus? Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 37(6), 607–616. PubMed 26866768. Quoted from the abstract; the full text is not yet in Eric’s library.

Read the result carefully, because a physician will. This is a comparison between groups, not an experiment that caused injury. It shows that injury goes with an inward, injury-focused attention and with worse performance. Gray’s own title asks it as a question. It is also baseball, not football. What it gives you is a name for what you see: not a strength problem, an attention problem. And an attention problem is a performance problem, which makes it yours to work on.

2. Why injury pulls attention inward

Singh, Gokeler and Benjaminse (2021) give the clinical version, after ACL reconstruction. “Loss of function, pain, fear of reinjury, and other psychological factors may cause a shift in focus towards the injured area such as the knee” (p. 1). The patient ends up “excessively focusing on the injured area.”

Javier Miler-Estrada, a movement coach who works with athletes after rehab, describes what that looks like when the athlete walks in. Many post-knee-injury athletes do their warm-up “with their gaze fixed on the ground, unaware and unable to perceive what is happening around them.” In his view the cause is often a rehab that spent months cueing the knee: avoid valgus, control the flexion. The result can be what he calls “fixed and frozen” movement.

Singh, H., Gokeler, A., & Benjaminse, A. (2021). Effective attentional focus strategies after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A commentary. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy, 16(6). doi:10.26603/001c.29848. Open access. Zotero EYKZD68B. Page numbers are pages of the PDF. A commentary, evidence level 5.
Miler-Estrada, J. (2023, April 30). Injury and affordance perception. Emergence blog. emergentmvmt.com. Practitioner writing, not peer-reviewed.

He adds one more link, citing a lab study: anxiety makes people underestimate what they are able to do (Graydon et al., 2012, as cited in Miler-Estrada, 2023; not yet read here). Put the three sources together and you have a chain you can say out loud:

LinkWhat it saysSource, and how strong
1. CausePain and fear of reinjury pull attention to the injured part.Singh et al. (2021), p. 1. Clinical commentary.
2. CostAthletes with attention on the injured part perform worse than healthy experts.Gray (2015). Peer-reviewed, between groups, baseball.
3. MechanismEyes on the body cannot pick up the game. Anxiety shrinks what he believes he can do.Miler-Estrada (2023). Practitioner, citing Graydon et al. (2012).

The rows are coloured as performer constraints, the first of the three constraint classes (performer, task, environment). Pain, fear and where attention goes belong to the athlete, and they shape what he can do just as much as strength does. You cannot see them on a force plate.

3. Fix one: the words you use

An internal focus points attention at the body: a joint, a limb, a movement. An external focus points it at the effect of the movement: the ground, the ball, the target, the sound of the landing. Singh and colleagues define it by what you say just before the rep: internally “on body part(s) and movement(s)” or externally “on intended movement effect” (p. 4).

The change is often a single word. Their example: a patient balancing on a Bosu is told “minimize movement of the feet” (internal). Change one word to “minimize movement of the Bosu” and the cue is external (p. 2).

The rule that makes this usable in a medical setting

You do not have to stop talking about the knee. Singh and colleagues split the goal from the cue (p. 4):

  • Before, explain the goal, body words allowed: “the goal of this exercise is to improve your knee bending while landing, as this promotes a softer landing, which is better for your knee.”
  • Just before the rep, give an external cue: “focus on landing with as little noise as possible,” or “pretend you are going to sit on a chair when landing.”

The knee still bends. The athlete gets there without watching it. This is how you keep the medical staff’s goal and still take the athlete’s eyes off the joint.

The trap: half-external cues

“Step toward the cone by pushing the floor away with your back foot” sounds external. Singh and colleagues say such hybrid cues “are not recommended”: the mention of a body part is a “self-invoking trigger” that pulls attention straight back inside. Their fix is small: say “back shoe” instead of “back foot,” and “shirt” instead of “shoulders” (p. 4).

Football versions

These rewrites are this course’s, built on Singh’s rules. They are not from the paper.

SituationInternal (avoid)External (use)
Receiver landing after a high-point, post-ACL“Bend your knees when you land.”“Land as quietly as you can.”
Cut after a knee injury“Don’t let your knee cave in.”“Push the grass away toward the sideline.”
Lineman’s pass set, back from an ankle“Stay low, bend at the knees.”“Keep your chest under his pads.”
Acceleration after a hamstring“Drive your knees up.”“Push the ground back behind you.”

4. Fix two: build the drill so no cue is needed

Better words are a real improvement, but they are still words. The ecological approach goes one step further: put something outside the athlete that he must deal with, and attention goes there on its own. Miler-Estrada’s version is to guide the athlete’s attention “towards focusing on the emerging movement problem in front of them” rather than on his own mechanics.

This is where lessons 0001 and 0002 meet. A live defender is the strongest external focus there is. You cannot mirror a DB’s hips while you watch your own knee. The opponent does the cueing for you. An unopposed drill has nothing outside the athlete to look at, so an anxious athlete looks at the one thing left: himself.

Miler-Estrada’s case is a football player. A high-school tight end, now playing Division 1, tore his ACL running routes. About ten months after surgery, his coaches took him out for his first field session against real opponents: full-speed routes against defenders, different coverages, high-school seniors and college players. During his warm-up he turned and said, nervously, “I haven’t worn these cleats since I tore my ACL.”

The session was controlled: “minimal incidental contact, no spectators present, and no score is kept.” Over later sessions they added field conditions, more defenders, a helmet and pads. His point is the direction of travel: “it is much better for our athletes to experience stress and anxiety gradually throughout the RTP process rather than to be thrown into the fire.” Do not shield the athlete from the game until clearance day. Give it to him in slices, with the pressure turned down. That is the simplify-don’t-decompose move from lesson 0001, applied to fear.

One rule for the data

Force plates, GPS and video tell you something about the athlete. Use them to decide what drill or constraint to set. Do not turn them into a cue. “Your left side is 12% down, push more through it” is an internal cue with a number attached. Measurements inform the constraint, never the cue. This is this course’s rule, adapted from how Rob Gray describes his own coaching; it is not a finding.

5. What the evidence does not say

  • Gray (2015) does not show that an internal focus causes reinjury. It shows worse performance, in baseball, compared between groups.
  • Singh et al. (2021) is a commentary, not a trial. Its strength is in the practical rules (goal before, external cue at the rep, no hybrids). It draws on the wider external-focus research for the claim that it helps.
  • Two schools, one direction. Singh’s paper comes from the external-focus research tradition (Gabriele Wulf’s work): it is about what you say. Ecological dynamics, the approach this course is built on, is about what is in the environment. They agree that attention should go outward. They disagree on why. You do not have to pick one to use both. Know which one you are citing.
  • “Gaze on the ground” is a practitioner’s observation, not a measurement. Use it as something to look for, not as proof.

6. The sentence for someone who was not there

Here is what the chain lets you say, in place of “he doesn’t look right.”

Template

“His [strength / running] numbers are back. What I am seeing is [hesitation before the plant, eyes down in warm-ups]. That fits a known pattern after injury: attention goes to the injured part, and performance drops even when strength is back (Gray, 2015; Singh et al., 2021). So I am not adding load. I am changing [the cue to an external one] and [putting a defender in the drill at reduced pressure], and I will tell you what changes over the next [five or six reps / three sessions].”

Notice what that sentence does. It names what you saw, cites why it matters, says what you will change, and promises something checkable. It turns a feeling into a plan.

7. Check yourself

Which cue is fully external?

What did Gray (2015) find in batters recovering from knee surgery?

A cleared receiver keeps his eyes down and hesitates in a pre-set cut drill. What is the best first move?

8. At practice tomorrow

Field task: a cue audit, then one drill change
  1. Record yourself. Put your phone in your pocket, recording, for one rehab session. (Tell the athlete, and do not record anything he would not want kept.)
  2. Afterwards, write down every cue you gave. Mark each one I (internal), E (external) or H (hybrid). Count them. Most clinicians are surprised by the I count.
  3. Rewrite your two most common internal cues as external ones. Keep the body part in the goal you say before the rep.
  4. In one drill, add something outside him to deal with: a defender at reduced pressure, a ball, a target, a teammate to beat to a spot. Stay inside what he is cleared for.
  5. Watch five or six reps. Write one line: where did his eyes go, and did the hesitation change?

Bring the I/E/H count and the one line to lesson 0003. If you still have your two lines from lesson 0001, compare them with this one line. Did adding an opponent change what you saw both times?

Primary source for this lesson

Singh, Gokeler & Benjaminse (2021). Effective attentional focus strategies after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. IJSPT. doi:10.26603/001c.29848. Free and open access. Read pages 1–2 for the problem and page 4 for the goal-then-cue rule and the hybrid trap. Harjiv Singh also writes from the ecological side of this field, so this is a good paper to know him by.

Also free, 15 minutes: Miler-Estrada, “Injury and Affordance Perception”, the tight-end case in full.

Cheat sheet for this lesson: reference/0002-attentional-focus.html. Print it and keep it where you plan sessions.

Anything unclear, a cue you cannot find an external version for, or a case this does not fit? Open this folder and ask. The agent that wrote this lesson is your teacher between sessions and can go back to the sources with you.

# Lesson 0002: attentional focus, taught as a chain plus two fixes

Eric asked for lesson 0002 on attentional focus on 2026-09-25, by `/teach` argument. It was the
natural next candidate recorded in learning record 0001. The lesson teaches the chain as
cause → cost → mechanism, and then two fixes:
1. **the words**: external cues, goal before and cue at the rep, no hybrids;
2. **the design**: put an opponent or target outside the athlete, so no cue is needed.

The second fix deliberately joins lesson 0002 back to lesson 0001: **the opponent does the
cueing.**

## Sources as used, with their limits stated in the lesson

- **Gray (2015).** Only the abstract has been read (Europe PMC); the full text is still not
  in the library. It is taught as association, in baseball, between groups. The lesson says
  so explicitly.
- **Singh, Gokeler & Benjaminse (2021)** (`EYKZD68B`) supplies the rules, with PDF pages
  1, 2 and 4 checked. It is labelled a level-5 commentary from the external-focus (Wulf)
  tradition, not ecological dynamics.
- **Miler-Estrada (2023)**, Emergence blog: the tight-end case and the "gaze on the ground"
  observation. Labelled practitioner writing.
- **Graydon et al. (2012)** is cited second-hand through Miler-Estrada and has not been read.

## Decisions

- The football cue rewrites are marked as this course's, not the paper's.
- "Measurements inform the constraint, never the cue" is stated as this course's rule
  (from `NOTES.md`, after Gray), not as a finding.
- The Wulf-vs-ecological split is named briefly and not litigated. Joe needs to know which
  school he is citing, not to referee them.
- `GLOSSARY.md` is still not created. Candidates flagged, not promoted: **internal focus**,
  **external focus**, **hybrid cue**, plus the two from 0001 (**opposed / unopposed**,
  **decompose vs simplify**). Promote a term when Joe uses it correctly.

## What is still unknown

- **Whether Joe completed the lesson 0001 field task.** No evidence has come back. Lesson
  0002 opens with a retrieval question on 0001, and its field task asks him to compare with
  his 0001 lines if he has them. **Before lesson 0003, ask for both field-task outputs.**
  Until then the zone of proximal development is a guess.
- No learning has been demonstrated yet. This record captures the decision.

## Next candidates

- Gray's connection-ball example: a task constraint as transition feedback, the "no cue
  names the body part" idea taken to its limit.
- Harries' reactivity ladder, re-read ecologically. See
  `docs/handoffs/2026-09-25-harries-velocity-bands.md`.
- Agility vs change-of-direction (Young et al. 2022 IUSCA position stand).

Constraints-led return to performance · Reference

Attentional focus

One page. The residue of lesson 0002.

The chain

LinkClaimSource
CausePain and fear of reinjury pull attention to the injured part.Singh et al. 2021, p. 1
CostAttention on the injured part goes with worse performance than healthy experts.Gray 2015 (association, baseball)
MechanismEyes on the body miss the game; anxiety shrinks what he thinks he can do.Miler-Estrada 2023 (practitioner)

Not a strength problem. An attention problem, and so a performance problem: yours to work on.

Two words

TermPoints attention atExample
InternalThe body: a joint, a limb, a movement“Bend your knees when you land.”
ExternalThe effect: ground, ball, target, sound“Land as quietly as you can.”
Hybrid (avoid)An effect plus a body part“Push off your back foot toward the cone.” Say “shoe”.

Three rules

  1. Goal before, cue at the rep. Explain the goal with body words if you need to. Just before the rep, give an external cue (Singh et al., p. 4).
  2. One word often does it. “Movement of the feet” → “movement of the Bosu” (p. 2).
  3. Measurements inform the constraint, never the cue. Force-plate or GPS numbers are for choosing the drill, not for telling the athlete. (This course’s rule.)

Better than a better cue

Put something outside him that he must deal with: a defender at reduced pressure, a ball, a target, a teammate to beat to a spot. The opponent does the cueing. An unopposed drill leaves an anxious athlete one thing to look at: himself. Give him the game in slices, with the pressure down; do not shield him until clearance day.

Football rewrites (this course’s, not the paper’s)

InternalExternalNo cue needed
“Don’t let your knee cave in.”“Push the grass away toward the sideline.”Beat a mirroring DB to the sideline.
“Stay low, bend at the knees.”“Keep your chest under his pads.”Rusher at half speed.
“Drive your knees up.”“Push the ground back behind you.”Chase down a ball carrier.

What to look for

Eyes down in warm-ups. Hesitation before the plant. Glances at the brace or the knee. A practitioner’s signs, not a measurement: something to check, not proof.

-<title>Lesson 0001 — The drill that hid the deficit</title>

-

Why a drill with no opponent cannot tell you an athlete is ready, what the opponent actually adds, and one sentence you can say to someone who was not there.
- About 40 minutes the way you work: read once, take notes, do the quiz, then plan the field task.

-

1. Start with a case you already own

-

In the interview you described a returning offensive lineman with a target game. You ran a needs assessment, worked a reverse calendar back from the game, and built run-blocking days, pass-blocking days and a reaction day. That method stays.

-

Then this happened. In the non-reactive drills he looked strong. He was experienced enough to time them up. In the reactive pass drills his performance dropped and he reported more strain. And at the end you could not load him at your own size, so a position coach and real defensive-line bodies had to finish the job.

-

You made a constraints argument without the vocabulary for it. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, one peer-reviewed paper to stand on, and a sentence you can say to a physician or a coordinator who was not at practice.

-

“He looked clean in the pre-set pass drill, so he is ready.” A clean rep in a drill with no opponent shows he can execute a plan he already knows. It does not show he can play football.

-

2. What the opponent is: information

-

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan and Otte (2025) put it in one line borrowed from Gibson: behavior affords behavior. How the other person moves is what shapes what the athlete can do next. In contact and invasion sports, the most useful information is tied to another body: the distance between them, his posture, how fast the gap is closing.

- Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., O Sullivan, M., & Otte, F. (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. Quest, 1–21. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759 — pp. 6–7. The Gibson line is The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), p. 135, as quoted there.

-

Now put that on a pass set. The lineman’s job is to pick up the rusher’s first step, his lean, the closing distance, and to set and re-anchor against it as it changes. Take the rusher away and there is nothing to pick up. The lineman sets to a plan instead. He can time it. That is why he looked strong. The drill did not lie to you. It just could not measure the thing you needed to know.

-

Parry and colleagues say it plainly: if opponents are not present, athletes “will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals” (p. 6). What is missing from the unopposed drill is not effort or load. It is the information the job runs on.

-

3. Two words, and two ways to make a drill easier

-

Unopposed practice isolates a skill and repeats it with no opponent present. Opposed practice keeps an opponent in the task, so the problem is alive: it changes moment to moment, it differs each time, and it cannot be fully predicted (Parry et al., 2025, pp. 2, 6). Those two words are the first glossary candidates in this course. Use them at practice this week.

-

Here is the part that changes how you regress a drill. There are two ways to make a task easier, and they are not the same.
-  <thead><tr><th>Move</th><th>What you do</th><th>What happens to the information</th></tr></thead>
- DecomposeTake a piece out. No rusher. Bag instead of a body. Cones instead of a defender.Gone. The athlete solves a different, smaller problem.
- SimplifyKeep the whole problem. Turn the pressure down. Rusher at half speed, hands behind his back, scripted first step.Still there. The athlete solves the real problem at a lower level.

-

Parry and colleagues give the second move directly: opposition “can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success” (p. 4). Rob Gray draws the same line between the two schools of coaching, decomposition on one side and simplification on the other; his table of comparative studies lists one head-to-head in volleyball where simplification beat decomposition. Treat that row as a pointer, not a citation, until the paper has been read.

- Gray, R. Two Approaches and Comparative Training Studies infographics, perceptionaction.com. Local copies: two-approaches.md (last row) and comparative-training-studies.md (study 17, Caldeira et al. 2023, volleyball). The comparative table is the page to bring when someone pushes back.
- This course’s extension, not the paper’s

-

In return to performance the reflex regression is to strip the drill to no opponent. On the logic above that does not simplify the task. It deletes it, and it deletes exactly the perception the returning athlete has to rebuild. Parry et al. write about skill development, not rehabilitation. Applying it to return to performance is our step, and you should say so when you cite it.

-

4. What the paper does not say

-

It does not say “never unopposed.” Read it fairly, because the first physician who has read it will.

-
  • Unopposed work has a place as exploration: a chance to search many ways of moving with little consequence, not to perfect one technique by repetition (pp. 3–6).

-
  • Unopposed drills can be made alive by putting other moving bodies in the same space, even when nobody is defending anyone (pp. 4–5).

-
  • There is “limited evidence to suggest that unopposed practice must precede opposed, game-like practice” (p. 6). The ladder you were taught is a habit, not a finding.

-

So the claim you can defend is narrower and stronger than “opposed is better.” It is this: an unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, because the information the athlete times up is the information that is missing. Use unopposed work to build capacity and to explore. Do not use it to prove anything.
- No opponentBodies in the spaceOpponent, pressure downLive opponent

-

Readiness lives on the right half of that bar. Regress along it. Do not jump off it.

-

The course’s anchor paper has the closest case to yours. Yearby, Myszka, Roberts, Woods and Davids (2024) worked with an NFL defensive end in the off-season. Instead of unopposed pass-rush technique, the task kept a centre, an offensive tackle and a quarterback on the field, so the rusher had to couple his movement to the snap and to the tackle’s set (p. 15). Over the off-season they saw new options emerge: an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, hand-chop variations (p. 18). Nobody taught those moves. The opponent did.

- Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. Free full text: Sheffield Hallam repository. Case observations, not a controlled trial.

-

Parry and colleagues do the same for running backs (pp. 11–16). A common “fit off the block” drill, usually run as a script, was rebuilt with a real blocker and a real defender, and then varied by changing who the opponent is, where each player starts, how big the space is, and whether a second defender pursues from depth. The cone drills they contrast it with, they say, “simply do not contain the relevant information that players will utilize” (p. 13).

-

A weekly habit worth starting: Shawn Myszka breaks down one NFL play a week as a movement problem at Football Beyond The Stats. Watch one, name the problem, name one constraint that would recreate it.

-

6. When you are not the right constraint

-

You said it yourself: you cannot load a lineman at your own size. Parry and colleagues give a ladder for who plays the opponent (p. 15):

-
  • Pair two position groups. Offensive line against defensive line. Both sides get a live problem.

-
  • Same position, other side of the ball. A second lineman plays the rusher.

-
  • A coach as the opponent. Less skilled, but “their presence still presents alive movement problems.”

-

Bringing in the position coach and defensive-line bodies was step one on that ladder. It was the right call. Now it has a name and a citation, and you can say it before someone asks why an athletic trainer needed the defensive line.

-

One more tool for the safety question, from a practitioner rather than a paper: scripted start, live finish. Fix how the rep begins so exposure is controlled; leave how it ends open so the perception stays. Alex Sarama, in interview with Rob Gray (Perception & Action Podcast, ep. 489). Practitioner opinion, cited as such.

-

7. The sentence for someone who was not there

-

This is the thing you said you were least confident about: defending a subjective call to an objective audience. Ask three questions of any drill you want to use as evidence.

-
  • What information did he have to pick up?

-
  • What did he have to do with it?

-

If the answer to the first question is “nothing,” the drill is not evidence. It may still be useful. It is not evidence.

-

“He had to read [the rusher’s first step and lean] and [set and re-anchor against it] with the rusher at [half speed, hands behind his back]. He did that in five of six reps. The pre-set drill could not show me that, because there was nothing in it to read.”

-

Those three questions are this course’s framing, built on Parry et al. They are not a quotation. The paper says a coach can ask “a number of pertinent questions” about a drill (p. 7); these are ours.

-

Answer from memory before you scroll back. Wrong answers come with the fix.

-

A returning lineman looks strong in a pre-set pass drill with no rusher. What does that result tell you?

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="It cannot tell you that. Live pass protection is coupling to a rusher, and there was no rusher to couple to. Ask question one: what did he have to read?">He is ready for live pass protection today.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="More reps of the same drill add more of the same thing. Add the missing information instead: one opponent, pressure turned down.">The drill needs more reps at higher speed.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Maybe, but that is a force-plate question. The drill measures whether he can execute a set he already knows, not what he can do against a moving body.">His strength has come back to full level.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-correct data-feedback="A known plan, executed well. Useful for capacity, not evidence of readiness. The information he would need to read in a game was not in the drill.">He can execute a pattern he already knows.</button>

-

You want to keep the rusher but make the task easier. Which change keeps the information in the drill?

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-correct data-feedback="That is simplification. The rusher still moves, so the lineman still has to read him. Parry et al. give the same move: constrain the opponent, do not remove him.">Keep the rusher, but restrict his first step.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="That is decomposition. A bag has no first step and no lean. Keep the body, and turn down what the body is allowed to do.">Replace the rusher with a padded bag instead.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Telling him the move removes the thing he has to read. If you need a controlled start, script the start and leave the finish live.">Tell the lineman exactly which move is coming.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="A rusher who does not move is a bag with a jersey. There is no first step to read. Let him move, at reduced speed or with hands behind his back.">Run the drill with the rusher standing still.</button>

-

According to Parry and colleagues, unopposed practice…

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="They say the opposite: there is limited evidence that unopposed must come first. Re-read section 4 and note the page number, p. 6.">must come before any opposed practice is used.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Too strong, and a physician who has read the paper will catch it. The paper keeps unopposed work as exploration. Narrow the claim: it is not evidence of readiness.">should be cut out of every football session.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-correct data-feedback="Exploration, capacity, and alive-unopposed work all have a place. What unopposed practice cannot do is show you the athlete can read an opponent.">has an exploring role, never a proving role.</button>

-  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Safest for load, maybe. But readiness is reading and acting on an opponent, and there is no opponent to read. Measure capacity here, not readiness.">is the safest place to measure true readiness.</button>
- Field task, with your current returning athlete

-
  • Pick one unopposed drill already in his plan.

-
  • Write one line: what information is missing from it? Use question one.

-
  • Add one opponent with the pressure turned down. Pick one: half speed, hands behind his back, or scripted start with a live finish.

-
  • Watch five or six reps. Change nothing while you watch.

-
  • Write one line: what did you see that the unopposed drill could not show?

-

Stay inside whatever he is already cleared for. This changes what the drill shows you, not how far along he is. If the opposed version would load him harder than the drill it replaces, turn the pressure down further, or check with Jacob or Tim first. Bring both lines to lesson 0002.

-

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan & Otte (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice. Quest. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759. Read pages 3–7 for the argument and 11–17 for the football case. The journal is paywalled; the PDF is in Eric’s Zotero, item key CA2CRR6Z. Two of the five authors wrote the football textbook this course is built on.

-

Free tonight: Yearby et al. (2024), the anchor paper, at the Sheffield Hallam repository. Start at the defensive-end case.

-
