+<title>Lesson 0001 — The drill that hid the deficit</title>

+

Why a drill with no opponent cannot tell you an athlete is ready, what the opponent actually adds, and one sentence you can say to someone who was not there.
+ About 40 minutes the way you work: read once, take notes, do the quiz, then plan the field task.

+

1. Start with a case you already own

+

In the interview you described a returning offensive lineman with a target game. You ran a needs assessment, worked a reverse calendar back from the game, and built run-blocking days, pass-blocking days and a reaction day. That method stays.

+

Then this happened. In the non-reactive drills he looked strong. He was experienced enough to time them up. In the reactive pass drills his performance dropped and he reported more strain. And at the end you could not load him at your own size, so a position coach and real defensive-line bodies had to finish the job.

+

You made a constraints argument without the vocabulary for it. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, one peer-reviewed paper to stand on, and a sentence you can say to a physician or a coordinator who was not at practice.

+

“He looked clean in the pre-set pass drill, so he is ready.” A clean rep in a drill with no opponent shows he can execute a plan he already knows. It does not show he can play football.

+

2. What the opponent is: information

+

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan and Otte (2025) put it in one line borrowed from Gibson: behavior affords behavior. How the other person moves is what shapes what the athlete can do next. In contact and invasion sports, the most useful information is tied to another body: the distance between them, his posture, how fast the gap is closing.

+ Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., O Sullivan, M., & Otte, F. (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. Quest, 1–21. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759 — pp. 6–7. The Gibson line is The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), p. 135, as quoted there.

+

Now put that on a pass set. The lineman’s job is to pick up the rusher’s first step, his lean, the closing distance, and to set and re-anchor against it as it changes. Take the rusher away and there is nothing to pick up. The lineman sets to a plan instead. He can time it. That is why he looked strong. The drill did not lie to you. It just could not measure the thing you needed to know.

+

Parry and colleagues say it plainly: if opponents are not present, athletes “will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals” (p. 6). What is missing from the unopposed drill is not effort or load. It is the information the job runs on.

+

3. Two words, and two ways to make a drill easier

+

Unopposed practice isolates a skill and repeats it with no opponent present. Opposed practice keeps an opponent in the task, so the problem is alive: it changes moment to moment, it differs each time, and it cannot be fully predicted (Parry et al., 2025, pp. 2, 6). Those two words are the first glossary candidates in this course. Use them at practice this week.

+

Here is the part that changes how you regress a drill. There are two ways to make a task easier, and they are not the same.
+  <thead><tr><th>Move</th><th>What you do</th><th>What happens to the information</th></tr></thead>
+ DecomposeTake a piece out. No rusher. Bag instead of a body. Cones instead of a defender.Gone. The athlete solves a different, smaller problem.
+ SimplifyKeep the whole problem. Turn the pressure down. Rusher at half speed, hands behind his back, scripted first step.Still there. The athlete solves the real problem at a lower level.

+

Parry and colleagues give the second move directly: opposition “can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success” (p. 4). Rob Gray draws the same line between the two schools of coaching, decomposition on one side and simplification on the other; his table of comparative studies lists one head-to-head in volleyball where simplification beat decomposition. Treat that row as a pointer, not a citation, until the paper has been read.

+ Gray, R. Two Approaches and Comparative Training Studies infographics, perceptionaction.com. Local copies: two-approaches.md (last row) and comparative-training-studies.md (study 17, Caldeira et al. 2023, volleyball). The comparative table is the page to bring when someone pushes back.
+ This course’s extension, not the paper’s

+

In return to performance the reflex regression is to strip the drill to no opponent. On the logic above that does not simplify the task. It deletes it, and it deletes exactly the perception the returning athlete has to rebuild. Parry et al. write about skill development, not rehabilitation. Applying it to return to performance is our step, and you should say so when you cite it.

+

4. What the paper does not say

+

It does not say “never unopposed.” Read it fairly, because the first physician who has read it will.

+
  • Unopposed work has a place as exploration: a chance to search many ways of moving with little consequence, not to perfect one technique by repetition (pp. 3–6).

+
  • Unopposed drills can be made alive by putting other moving bodies in the same space, even when nobody is defending anyone (pp. 4–5).

+
  • There is “limited evidence to suggest that unopposed practice must precede opposed, game-like practice” (p. 6). The ladder you were taught is a habit, not a finding.

+

So the claim you can defend is narrower and stronger than “opposed is better.” It is this: an unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, because the information the athlete times up is the information that is missing. Use unopposed work to build capacity and to explore. Do not use it to prove anything.
+ No opponentBodies in the spaceOpponent, pressure downLive opponent

+

Readiness lives on the right half of that bar. Regress along it. Do not jump off it.

+

The course’s anchor paper has the closest case to yours. Yearby, Myszka, Roberts, Woods and Davids (2024) worked with an NFL defensive end in the off-season. Instead of unopposed pass-rush technique, the task kept a centre, an offensive tackle and a quarterback on the field, so the rusher had to couple his movement to the snap and to the tackle’s set (p. 15). Over the off-season they saw new options emerge: an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, hand-chop variations (p. 18). Nobody taught those moves. The opponent did.

+ Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. Free full text: Sheffield Hallam repository. Case observations, not a controlled trial.

+

Parry and colleagues do the same for running backs (pp. 11–16). A common “fit off the block” drill, usually run as a script, was rebuilt with a real blocker and a real defender, and then varied by changing who the opponent is, where each player starts, how big the space is, and whether a second defender pursues from depth. The cone drills they contrast it with, they say, “simply do not contain the relevant information that players will utilize” (p. 13).

+

A weekly habit worth starting: Shawn Myszka breaks down one NFL play a week as a movement problem at Football Beyond The Stats. Watch one, name the problem, name one constraint that would recreate it.

+

6. When you are not the right constraint

+

You said it yourself: you cannot load a lineman at your own size. Parry and colleagues give a ladder for who plays the opponent (p. 15):

+
  • Pair two position groups. Offensive line against defensive line. Both sides get a live problem.

+
  • Same position, other side of the ball. A second lineman plays the rusher.

+
  • A coach as the opponent. Less skilled, but “their presence still presents alive movement problems.”

+

Bringing in the position coach and defensive-line bodies was step one on that ladder. It was the right call. Now it has a name and a citation, and you can say it before someone asks why an athletic trainer needed the defensive line.

+

One more tool for the safety question, from a practitioner rather than a paper: scripted start, live finish. Fix how the rep begins so exposure is controlled; leave how it ends open so the perception stays. Alex Sarama, in interview with Rob Gray (Perception & Action Podcast, ep. 489). Practitioner opinion, cited as such.

+

7. The sentence for someone who was not there

+

This is the thing you said you were least confident about: defending a subjective call to an objective audience. Ask three questions of any drill you want to use as evidence.

+
  • What information did he have to pick up?

+
  • What did he have to do with it?

+

If the answer to the first question is “nothing,” the drill is not evidence. It may still be useful. It is not evidence.

+

“He had to read [the rusher’s first step and lean] and [set and re-anchor against it] with the rusher at [half speed, hands behind his back]. He did that in five of six reps. The pre-set drill could not show me that, because there was nothing in it to read.”

+

Those three questions are this course’s framing, built on Parry et al. They are not a quotation. The paper says a coach can ask “a number of pertinent questions” about a drill (p. 7); these are ours.

+

Answer from memory before you scroll back. Wrong answers come with the fix.

+

A returning lineman looks strong in a pre-set pass drill with no rusher. What does that result tell you?

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="It cannot tell you that. Live pass protection is coupling to a rusher, and there was no rusher to couple to. Ask question one: what did he have to read?">He is ready for live pass protection today.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="More reps of the same drill add more of the same thing. Add the missing information instead: one opponent, pressure turned down.">The drill needs more reps at higher speed.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Maybe, but that is a force-plate question. The drill measures whether he can execute a set he already knows, not what he can do against a moving body.">His strength has come back to full level.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-correct data-feedback="A known plan, executed well. Useful for capacity, not evidence of readiness. The information he would need to read in a game was not in the drill.">He can execute a pattern he already knows.</button>

+

You want to keep the rusher but make the task easier. Which change keeps the information in the drill?

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-correct data-feedback="That is simplification. The rusher still moves, so the lineman still has to read him. Parry et al. give the same move: constrain the opponent, do not remove him.">Keep the rusher, but restrict his first step.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="That is decomposition. A bag has no first step and no lean. Keep the body, and turn down what the body is allowed to do.">Replace the rusher with a padded bag instead.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Telling him the move removes the thing he has to read. If you need a controlled start, script the start and leave the finish live.">Tell the lineman exactly which move is coming.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="A rusher who does not move is a bag with a jersey. There is no first step to read. Let him move, at reduced speed or with hands behind his back.">Run the drill with the rusher standing still.</button>

+

According to Parry and colleagues, unopposed practice…

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="They say the opposite: there is limited evidence that unopposed must come first. Re-read section 4 and note the page number, p. 6.">must come before any opposed practice is used.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Too strong, and a physician who has read the paper will catch it. The paper keeps unopposed work as exploration. Narrow the claim: it is not evidence of readiness.">should be cut out of every football session.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-correct data-feedback="Exploration, capacity, and alive-unopposed work all have a place. What unopposed practice cannot do is show you the athlete can read an opponent.">has an exploring role, never a proving role.</button>

+  <button class="quiz__opt" data-feedback="Safest for load, maybe. But readiness is reading and acting on an opponent, and there is no opponent to read. Measure capacity here, not readiness.">is the safest place to measure true readiness.</button>
+ Field task, with your current returning athlete

+
  • Pick one unopposed drill already in his plan.

+
  • Write one line: what information is missing from it? Use question one.

+
  • Add one opponent with the pressure turned down. Pick one: half speed, hands behind his back, or scripted start with a live finish.

+
  • Watch five or six reps. Change nothing while you watch.

+
  • Write one line: what did you see that the unopposed drill could not show?

+

Stay inside whatever he is already cleared for. This changes what the drill shows you, not how far along he is. If the opposed version would load him harder than the drill it replaces, turn the pressure down further, or check with Jacob or Tim first. Bring both lines to lesson 0002.

+

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan & Otte (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice. Quest. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759. Read pages 3–7 for the argument and 11–17 for the football case. The journal is paywalled; the PDF is in Eric’s Zotero, item key CA2CRR6Z. Two of the five authors wrote the football textbook this course is built on.

+

+

lines: Singh, Gokeler and Benjaminse (2021) give the clinical version, after ACL reconstruction. “Loss of function, pain, fear of reinjury, and other psychological factors may cause a shift in focus towards the injured area such as the knee” (p. 1). The patient ends up “excessively focusing on the injured area.”

-

Javier Miler-Estrada, a movement coach who works with athletes after rehab, describes what that looks like when the athlete walks in. Many post-knee-injury athletes do their warm-up “with their gaze fixed on the ground, unaware and unable to perceive what is happening around them.” In his view the cause is often a rehab that spent months cueing the knee: avoid valgus, control the flexion. The result can be what he calls “fixed and frozen” movement.

+

Many post-knee-injury athletes do their warm-up “with their gaze fixed on the ground, unaware and unable to perceive what is happening around them.” In his observation the cause is often “an overemphasis and hyperfocus on their biomechanics” during rehab, with cues aimed at the knee itself: avoid valgus, avoid excessive flexion. The result can be what he calls “fixed and frozen” movement.

Lesson 0002, "Attention goes where you point it", is written and open in your browser. It's on branch `claude/lesson-0002-attentional-focus`, in PR #2, which isn't merged yet. I rendered it in Chrome and checked it by eye, and checked the Singh quotes against pages 1, 2 and 4 of the PDF.

**What it teaches Joe** (about 35 minutes at his pace):
- **Warm-up:** one quiz question on lesson 0001, answered from memory.
- **The problem:** the athlete who tests fine and plays wrong. It rests on three sources:
  - Gray (2015): athletes recovering from surgery had attention fixed on the injured area and performed worse than healthy experts. It's taught as "goes with", not "causes", and it's baseball.
  - Singh et al. (2021): pain and fear of reinjury pull attention toward the injured part.
  - Miler-Estrada's Emergence post: the "eyes on the ground" observation and the tight end who tore his ACL.
- **Fix one, the words:** cue the effect, not the body part. Explain the goal before the rep, even in body terms, and give an outward cue at the rep. Don't mix the two: "back *foot*" becomes "back *shoe*". Football rewrites of common cues are labelled as the course's own.
- **Fix two, the drill:** put a defender in, with the pressure turned down, and he can't watch his knee. The opponent does the cueing. This ties lesson 0002 back to 0001.
- **Honest limits:** what each source does and doesn't show, and a one-line note on the two schools of thought behind the advice.
- **The template sentence** for "he doesn't look right", three quizzes, and a field task. Joe records one session on his phone, sorts every cue he gave as internal, external or mixed, rewrites his two most common internal cues, and adds an opponent to one drill.

**Files, all in `RTP_Constraints_Course`:**
- `lessons/0002-attention-goes-where-you-point-it.html`
- `reference/0002-attentional-focus.html` (printable cheat sheet)
- `learning-records/0002-lesson-0002-attentional-focus.md`

- The Gray (2015) paper is quoted from its abstract only; it isn't in your library yet. Getting the full text is on the status list.
- I don't know whether Joe did the lesson 0001 field task. Collect both field-task results before lesson 0003, or the next lesson's difficulty is a guess.

content.text:
PR #2 is merged into `main` (merge commit `008b478`).

On your question, here's what I found and what I recommend.

**What we know about delivery.** In the interview, Joe said he'd do the lessons himself on his laptop in the office (42:45). Nobody asked whether he has Claude. That matters, because every lesson ends with "open this folder and ask the agent, it's your teacher." Without Claude on his side, that line doesn't work.

**Should we build the whole course now? No: map it now, build one lesson ahead.**
- The course is designed to pick each next lesson from what Joe actually shows he's learned. So far there's no evidence either way; we don't know if he did the lesson 0001 field task. Writing six more lessons now means guessing his level six times.
- Your own rule from the self-audit says ship to a named person and check it sticks before building more. Two lessons he hasn't touched yet is the test.
- What does help now is a **course map**: about 8 lessons, one line each, so Joe sees where it's going and you can show Jacob and Tim the full arc. That takes me about an hour, not days.

**How to deliver it.**
- **Recommended: an offline package in a shared Drive folder.** I write a small script that copies only the shareable parts (lessons, cheat sheets, assets, a front page) into a folder Joe opens by double-clicking. Quizzes work offline. It strips what can't leave:
  - links to the interview transcript, which names athletes;
  - Rob Gray's infographics, which we agreed not to republish;
  - the Myszka book.

  Updates reach him when you re-run the script. He sends field-task answers back in one notes doc. No IT approval is needed.
- **The most powerful option: Joe runs it with Claude himself.** He'd get the repo and type `/teach`, and the agent would really be his teacher, as the lessons promise. It needs a Claude license and Baylor IT sign-off. Worth doing later, not first.
- **A hosted website: no.** Public hosting would publish copyrighted material and the course's athlete context. Private hosting needs IT approval. It adds nothing the Drive folder doesn't.

Two decisions from you before I build:

## THE TEXTBOOK

- **Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Gray, R.** *Enhancing Skill in American Football: Revolutionizing Practice Design for Transfer to Game Day.* ISBN 9798298178846. [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Enhancing-skill-American-football-Revolutionizing/dp/B0FMQWN1NK)
  **Three of the four named practitioners, one book, this exact topic, this exact sport.** Eric owns a paper copy as of 2026-09-01. This should be the spine of the course, ahead of every journal paper below. **BEFORE SCANNING ANYTHING: check whether a Kindle edition exists (ASIN B0FMQWN1NK) — a digital copy removes the scan, the OCR and the whole `ocrmypdf` route in one step. Unverified as of 2026-09-02; see the American-football section below.** Otherwise ingest via the `ingest-book` skill once scanned — scanning route in `NOTES.md`.

  Myszka's other titles (*The Problem-Solving Athlete* series: *Coaching the Problem-Solving Athlete*, *Become One With the Game*, *The Lifelong Athlete*) are adjacent but not football-specific. Skip unless the mission widens.

## Knowledge — Anchor sources (already in the library)

- **Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024).** Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. *Sports Coaching Review, 13*(3), 362–385. [doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698](https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698) · `key=7M8YQMKU`
  `LIB/yearby-2024-applying-an-ecological-approach-to-practice-design-in-american-football-some-case-examples.md`
  **The single most on-mission paper in the library.** Translates ecological dynamics, representative learning design, and the CLA into two concrete American-football cases. Use for: the whole spine of the course; every worked football example.

- **Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Davids, K. (2024).** *Being Water*: How key ideas from the practice of Bruce Lee align with contemporary theorizing in movement skill acquisition. *Sport, Education and Society*. [doi:10.1080/13573322.2022.2160701](https://doi.org/10.1080/13573322.2022.2160701)
  `LIB/myszka-2024-i-being-water-i-how-key-ideas-from-the-practice-of-bruce-lee-align-with-contemporary-theor.md`
  Use for: adaptability as the goal rather than a repeatable ideal technique. Good rhetorical ammunition for the coach conversation.

- **Rob Gray — *How We Learn to Move: A Revolution in the Way We Coach & Practice Sports Skills*** (2021). **NOT YET IN THE LIBRARY — acquire.**
  Use for: Joe's primary self-study text. Plain-language introduction to ecological dynamics, the CLA, and differential learning. Pair with the *Perception & Action* podcast back-catalogue.

## Knowledge — What the football job actually demands (already in the library)

Representative design is impossible without knowing the real demands. This cluster is
the evidence for "what does this position actually have to do".

- **Novak, A. R., et al. (2021).** Analysis of the worst-case scenarios in an elite football team. *Journal of Sports Sciences, 39*(16), 1850–1859. [doi:10.1080/02640414.2021.1902138](https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2021.1902138)
  `LIB/novak-2021-analysis-of-the-worst-case-scenarios-in-an-elite-football-team-towards-a-better-understand.md`
  Use for: setting the ceiling a drill must eventually reach. (Soccer, but the method transfers.)

- **Iosia, M. F., & Bishop, P. A. (2008).** Analysis of exercise-to-rest ratios during Division IA televised football competition. *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 22*(2), 332–340. [doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31816607b0](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e31816607b0)
  `LIB/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition.md`
  Use for: American-football work:rest structure — a task constraint Joe can set precisely.

- **Young, W., Dos'Santos, T., Harper, D., Jeffreys, I., & Talpey, S. (2022).** Agility in invasion sports: Position stand of the IUSCA. *International Journal of Strength and Conditioning*. [doi:10.47206/ijsc.v2i1.126](https://doi.org/10.47206/ijsc.v2i1.126) · `key=R656I7IY`
  **Check this before writing lesson 0001.** `NOTES.md` builds a candidate hook on *"agility and change-of-direction speed are independent skills," attributed to Young 2015.* Same lead author, eight years later, four co-authors, a formal **position stand**, and specifically about **invasion sports** — i.e. football. **Verify which paper actually makes the claim and cite the stronger one.**
  `LIB/young-2022-agility-in-invasion-sports-position-stand-of-the-iusca.md`
  Use for: the formal case that agility requires a perceptual stimulus. The bridge between the S&C literature and ecological dynamics.

- **Young, W., et al. (2015).** Agility and change of direction speed are independent skills.
  `LIB/young-2015-agility-and-change-of-direction-speed-are-independent-skills-implications-for-training-for.md`
  Use for: the single cleanest citation for "your cone drill is not agility."

- **Mokha, M. (n.d.).** American football position does not influence symmetry in joint power during high-speed running.
  `LIB/mokha-undated-american-football-position-does-not-influence-symmetry-in-joint-power-during-high-speed-ru.md`
  Use for: caution about symmetry metrics as a readiness proxy.

### The published critique — football-specific, and better than the generic rebuttal already listed

- **Bobrownicki, R., Carson, H. J., MacPherson, A. C., et al. (2022).** Constraints of the constraints-led approach in American football and comments on Yearby et al. (2022). *Sports Coaching Review, 15*(1), 46–58. [doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579](https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579) · [Edinburgh Research Explorer](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/constraints-of-the-constraints-led-approach-in-american-football-/)
  **A direct, peer-reviewed rebuttal to this course's anchor paper (`7M8YQMKU`), in this exact sport, in the same journal.** The authors (University of Edinburgh) accept the CLA is a useful tool but argue that **as a standalone approach it carries mechanistic and epistemological problems that block experimental comparison and limit its novelty and real-world applicability**, and that drawing on a **wider set of theoretical perspectives** serves practitioners better.
  **This supersedes Fransen (`CBJGJQX5`) as the rebuttal to teach.** Fransen argues against skill-acquisition specialists in general; **this argues against this specific paper, about this specific sport.** **Teach the anchor paper and this together, in the same lesson.** A practitioner who has only heard the case *for* folds the first time a physician or coordinator pushes back — and the pushback he meets will look like this one.
  **Related:** *The adaptable coach — a critical review of the practical implications for traditional and constraints-led approaches in sport coaching* ([ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/379382191)) — a second critical review, not yet assessed.

### The anchor paper is free

- **The Version of Record of Yearby et al. is openly available** at Sheffield Hallam's repository: [shura.shu.ac.uk/30272](https://shura.shu.ac.uk/30272/1/Davids-ApplyingEcologicalApproach%28VoR%29.pdf). **Joe can read the anchor paper without a paywall or a library login.** Also on [Academia.edu](https://www.academia.edu/78122686/) and [ResearchGate](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/359706952).

input.content:
Constraints-led return to performance · Reference

Course map

Where the course is going, lesson by lesson. Each lesson answers one question you will be asked by someone who was not there, and ends in something you can do at practice the next day.

Lessons are written one at a time, after the field task from the last one comes back. The order below is the plan, not a promise: what you find in your field tasks can move a lesson earlier, later, or out. Last revised 2026-09-25.

The arc

See it (1–2)Name it (3–4)Dose it (5–6)Defend it (7–8)

First you learn to see what a drill hides. Then you get the words to name what you are changing. Then you learn to dose a change: how hard, how often, when to progress. Last, you learn to defend it to a physician, a coordinator, or a skeptic with a paper.

Lessons

#The question it answersWhat you will be able to doAnchor sources
1 Why did the drill flatter him? Say why an unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, and simplify a drill without deleting the opponent. Parry et al. 2025; Yearby et al. 2024 Built
2 Why does he test fine and play wrong? Spot attention stuck on the injury, rewrite internal cues as external ones, and let an opponent do the cueing. Gray 2015; Singh et al. 2021; Miler-Estrada 2023 Built
3 What exactly am I changing? Name the three constraint classes (performer, task, environment) and turn each one up or down on purpose. Myszka, Yearby & Gray (textbook); Yearby et al. 2024 Planned
4 Does this drill look like his job? State what a position has to read and do, and judge whether a drill samples it. Why a cone drill is not agility. Yearby et al. 2024; Young et al. 2022 (IUSCA agility); textbook Planned
5 When do I make it harder? Use his success rate as the dial for progressing or regressing a drill, and read the control-to-chaos continuum ecologically. Gray, 3 Questions; Allen et al. 2021; Taberner et al. 2025 Planned
6 How much, and on which day? Put a constraint change into your reverse calendar so a “chaotic” drill is not an accidental load spike. Speed bands from the velocity sheet. Taberner et al. 2022; Harries (Sportsmith); Baylor velocity-band sheet Planned
7 Who plays the opponent, and what about the acute case? Know when you are not the right constraint, and apply everything to the player who is never held out. Parry et al. 2025; Taberner et al., NBA “on the road” Planned
8 How do I defend this to a skeptic? Answer the published critique of this approach, and the two objections you expect: “every trainer should do this” and “this belongs in the weight room.” Bobrownicki et al. 2022; Yearby et al. 2024; Fransen 2026 Planned

After lesson 8

The lessons become the specification for a drill-design tool: you enter the position, injury, phase and what you are trying to expose, and it returns a session plan in under ten minutes. It is built with you, from your field tasks, and it runs locally.

How each lesson works

  1. Read it once and take notes. Each lesson is sized for the way you study, 30 to 40 minutes.
  2. Do the quiz from memory. Wrong answers tell you how to fix them.
  3. Run the field task at practice.
  4. Write what you saw in your field notes. That is what the next lesson is built from.

#!/usr/bin/env python3 """Export the shareable part of the course into a folder Joe opens offline. What goes out: lessons/*.html, reference/*.html (not its subfolders), assets/*.css and *.js, plus a generated index.html front page. What never goes out, and how it is enforced: - interviews/ (names athletes), sources/ (the Myszka book), reference/gray-infographics/ (do not republish), MISSION.md, NOTES.md and every other .md file. entries.description:
Call this tool to create or upload a File to Google Drive.

If uploading content, prefer `textContent` for text content. For non-UTF8 contents, use the `base64Content` field and base64 encode the data to set on that field.

Returns a single File object upon successful creation.

The following Google first-party mime types can be created without providing content:

 - `application/vnd.google-apps.document` 
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.spreadsheet` 
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.presentation` 

Folders can be created by setting the mime type to `application/vnd.google-apps.folder`.

When uploading content, the `contentMimeType` field is required and should match the type of the content being uploaded.

By default, supported content will be converted to Google first-party mime types.

To disable conversions for first-party mime types, set `disableConversionToGoogleType` to true.

base64Content.description: Optional. The base64 encoded content to upload. It's an error to set this and `textContent`.

content.description: Deprecated: Use `base64Content` or `textContent` instead. The content of the file encoded as base64. The content field should always be base64 encoded regardless of the mime type of the file.

contentMimeType.description: The mime type of the content being uploaded. Required when any type of content is provided.

disableConversionToGoogleType.description: Set to true to retain the passed in content mime type and not convert to a Google type. For example, without this a `text/plain` content mime type will be converted to to `application/vnd.google-apps.document`. Has no effect for types that do not have a Google equivalent.

mimeType.description: Deprecated: DO NOT USE!! Set `contentMimeType` instead.

parentId.description: The parent id of the file.

textContent.description: Optional. The (UTF-8) text content to upload. It's an error to set this and `base64Content`.

title.description: Required. The title of the file.

entries.description:
Search for Drive files using a structured query (syntax: `query_term operator values`). Only terms in this list are supported.
Combine clauses with `and`, `or`, `not`, and parentheses. String values must be single-quoted; escape embedded quotes as `\'`.
Context window token management can be tuned via `snippetVerbosity` (default is `SnippetVerbosity.DETAILED`) or if only metadata is needed, use `excludeContentSnippets`.

Do NOT include document type terms (e.g., 'presentation', 'slides', 'deck', 'document', 'doc', 'spreadsheet', 'sheet', 'pdf', 'folder') inside `title contains '...'` or `fullText contains '...'` clauses. Separate title keywords from file type terms. Instead map them to `mimeType` clauses in the query (e.g., 'slides' -> `mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.presentation'`).

Query terms & operators:

 - `title` (ops: contains, =, !=) — file title
 - `fullText` (ops: contains) — title or body text
 - `mimeType` (ops: contains, =, !=) — MIME type
 - `modifiedTime`, `viewedByMeTime`, `createdTime` (ops: `<=`, `<`, `=`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`). Use RFC 3339 UTC, e.g., `2012-06-04T12:00:00-08:00`. Date types not comparable.
 - `parentId` (ops: `=`, `!=`). Use `'root'` for the user's "My Drive".
 - `owner` (ops: `=`, `!=`). Use `'me'` for the requesting user.
 - `sharedWithMe` (ops: `=`, `!=`). Values: `true` or `false`.

Other operators: `and`, `or`, `not`.

Examples:

 - `title contains 'hello' and title contains 'goodbye'`
 - `modifiedTime > '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z' and (mimeType contains 'image/' or mimeType contains 'video/')`
 - `parentId = '1234567'`
 - `fullText contains 'hello'`
 - `owner = 'test@example.org'`
 - `sharedWithMe = true`
 - `owner = 'me'` (for files owned by the user)

Use `next_page_token` to paginate. An empty response means no more results.

pageSize.description: The maximum number of files to return in each page.

pageToken.description: The page token to use for pagination.

snippetVerbosity.description: Optional. Set to specify how verbose the snippets should be. Defaults to DETAILED if not set.

Constraints-led return to performance

Write what you saw after each field task. Short is fine. The next lesson is built from this page. Use position and injury, not athlete names.

What I added (half speed / hands behind back / scripted start, live finish):
Line 2 - What did I see that the unopposed drill could not show?
Questions:

Lesson 0002 - Attention goes where you point it
Date:
Cue count from my recorded session:  Internal ___   External ___   Hybrid ___
My two most common internal cues, rewritten as external:
1.
2.

One line - Where did his eyes go, and did the hesitation change?
Compare with my lesson 0001 lines - did adding an opponent change what I saw both times?

lines: -A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
-**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
-**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
-phase of return to performance in American football.
-Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
-`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
-slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.
-Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
-| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
-| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |

-| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
-| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
-| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
-| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. 0001 written 2026-09-03 (opposed vs unopposed). |
-| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. |

-| `reference/gray-infographics/` | Local copies of Rob Gray's free infographics, saved 2026-09-03 because the site is one person's. Includes the 21-study comparative table, extracted and searchable. **Do not republish, do not commit.** See its `README.md`. |

-| `sources/` | Full-text books and long PDFs obtained legitimately. Author-supplied — **never redistribute, never commit.** Holds the Myszka book (240 pages, printed 14–253), its OCR text sidecar, the reversible scan manifest, and the extracted bibliography. |

-| `scripts/` | `velocity_band_sheet.py` builds the Baylor velocity-band sheet (Harries' levels from GPS; writes to Drive only, since it names athletes). Also the book-scan pipeline. `scan_pipeline.py` turns phone photos into a page-ordered OCR'd PDF and **refuses to rename unless the arithmetic gate passes**; `verify_pdf.py` proves page order afterwards by an independent route. Read `scan_pipeline.py`'s docstring before the next scanning job — it carries every trap found so far. |
-| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. 0001 records the lesson-0001 hook decision and Joe's starting floor. |
-- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
-  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
-- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.
-- **Every lesson ends in something Joe could do at practice tomorrow.**
-- `GLOSSARY.md` does not exist yet by design — see `NOTES.md`.
-- **Phase 2 is a drill-design tool.** Do not start it until the lessons have specified it.
-Search with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`. Zotero MCP was down on 2026-09-01.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.
